If you prefer over-ear headphones, Amazon has also listed the AirPods Max 2 for $419 in the U.S., $130 off and just $20 above the lowest price we’ve tracked.
If you prefer an open-ear fit, AirPods 5 are the cheaper option: in the U.K. we’ve seen £20 off the wireless charging AirPods 5, at £119, while it was still at its regular $149 U.S. price at our last check. Below, we explain which AirPods to choose and how the offers compare with previous discounts. For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our Apple Black Friday deals roundups of the best Mac deals, iPad deals, and Apple Watch deals.
Apple’s own Black Friday offer runs November 27–30, 2026. Buy eligible AirPods directly from Apple, and you’ll receive a gift card to use on a future purchase. More details here: Apple Black Friday 2026: Up to $300/£240 in gift cards – full list of eligible products.




Which AirPods should you buy this Black Friday?


AirPods Pro 3 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Pro 3 are especially worth considering if you want strong noise cancellation, a secure in-ear fit, or Apple’s hearing-health features. Their foam-infused ear tips help improve the fit, while an in-ear heart-rate sensor adds another reason to choose them over standard AirPods. Battery life is rated at up to eight hours with noise cancellation enabled.
For most buyers looking for noise-isolating earbuds, these would be our first choice. Older AirPods Pro 2 are worth considering only when the clearance savings are substantial.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has slashed $100 off the AirPods Pro 3, to just $149, the same price as the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case and below their previous all-time low of $169. Amazon sold out for a day or so, but got more stock; if that happens again, Walmart also has them at that price.
U.K. Black Friday price: Earlier in November, AirPods Pro 3 were £30 off in the U.K., before rising to £200, then dropping down to £174, only to return to £200. Amazon now has the AirPods Pro 3 for £155.98, £63.02 off the £219 RRP! We recommend being quick because that price is going up and down like a Swanee whistle.
Apple’s deal: You can get a $50/£40 gift card with your purchase. 






AirPods 5 – Best for buyers who prefer earbuds without silicone tips

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods 5 offer a lower-cost entry point and an open-ear design for people who don’t like silicone-tipped earbuds. They include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, alongside Transparency mode and Adaptive Audio.
Check which charging case you’re buying. The Wireless Charging Case package adds wireless charging, longer battery life, a Find My speaker, and volume adjustment by swiping the stems. It’s our preferred package when the price difference is small.
U.S. Black Friday price: We’ve not seen a discount yet on the AirPods 5.
U.K. Black Friday price:  You can get £20 off the AirPods 5 with wireless charging in the U.K. That’s the same as Apple’s gift card ‘saving’.
Apple’s deal: Get a $25/£20 gift card with the purchase of AirPods 5.






AirPods Max 2 – Best for over-ear listening

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Max 2 are the option to consider if you specifically want over-ear headphones. The March 2026 update introduced Apple’s H2 chip and improved noise cancellation, while retaining the premium design and a choice of colors.
We find them difficult to recommend at full price, so the size of the discount matters. Compare any offer with previous sale prices rather than judging it solely against Apple’s asking price.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has the AirPods Max 2 for $419, a $130 saving.
U.K. Black Friday price:  AirPods Max 2 were reduced to £449 at Amazon, but they are now back at the full £499. From November 27, Apple will include a £60 gift card with AirPods Max purchases. 
Apple’s deal: Get a $75/£60 gift card with the purchase of AirPods Max 2. 






Other headphones – Worthy AirPods alternatives

				
					

				
			
Beats




If AirPods aren’t in your budget, Apple also sells a line of Beats headphones and earbuds that offer many of the same features for a lower price, including the popular on-ear Solo 4 and Powerbeats Pro 2. We’ll also track headphone deals in our roundup of the best earbuds for iPhone and best over-ear headphones if you’d like to see deals on other brands.

U.K. Black Friday price:  There is £90 off the Powerbeats Pro 2 and £100 off the Powerbeats Fit at Amazon, but we expect to see more discounts later in November.

Should you buy AirPods now or wait for a better deal?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need AirPods immediately. But the sales now stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer is close to a model’s previous low, it can be worth taking: last year’s best deals frequently sold out, and popular offers could go quickly again.
Previous sale prices provide useful benchmarks. At $149, AirPods Pro 3 are $20 below the previous low we tracked, while AirPods Max 2 fell to $399 during June Prime Day. An offer above those prices may still be worth considering, but a reduction from Apple’s regular price doesn’t automatically make it an exceptional deal.
For AirPods 5, waiting for a discount makes sense if you aren’t in a hurry: they didn’t receive a significant reduction during October Prime Day. With AirPods Max 2, we’d hold out for a substantial saving rather than pay full price.
Compare retailers, too. Amazon isn’t always cheapest: Walmart and Best Buy also compete on AirPods pricing, while Argos offered competitive U.K. deals last year. Our guide to the best time to buy AirPods has more advice on purchase timing.






Should you buy an old pair of AirPods? 
Older-generation AirPods can be a good buy at the right clearance price. Compare their actual selling price with the discounted price of their replacement, rather than focusing on the percentage saving from an old launch price. A substantial discount can make an older pair worthwhile; a small difference may leave you sacrificing useful features for little saving.
AirPods 4 are harder to recommend now that AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, starting at the same $129 price previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC. Check which AirPods 4 version you’re buying—there were models with and without noise cancellation—and look for a substantial saving over AirPods 5.
AirPods Pro 2 remain worth considering if they’re significantly cheaper than Pro 3. However, the newer model improves fit, noise cancellation, and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing. Compare their sale prices carefully: a strong Pro 3 discount could make the older pair’s clearance offer less attractive.
The original AirPods Max also need a substantial discount to justify choosing them over Max 2. The newer headphones add the H2 chip, improved noise cancellation, and features including Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. Check the generation rather than relying on the charging port alone: the original AirPods Max were also sold in a USB-C version.
Buying older stock new is different from buying used or refurbished AirPods. For those pairs, check the stated condition, charging case, warranty, and returns policy, and buy from a reputable seller. Be cautious about battery condition and unusually low marketplace prices, since convincing counterfeits can resemble genuine AirPods. Our guide explains how to spot fake AirPods.
For more advice, see our AirPods buying guide and guide to the best time to buy AirPods.






AirPods deals to avoid

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Check exactly what an offer includes before comparing prices. Different charging-case packages can affect features and value, so make sure you’re comparing equivalent versions. Also check any spending requirements, contracts, or rebates attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods.
Judge the price against previous selling prices as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.
Check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair. For used or refurbished AirPods, look for clear information about condition, warranty, and returns coverage. Battery condition deserves particular caution: a low purchase price may be less attractive if listening time has deteriorated.
Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Unusually low prices from unfamiliar sellers warrant caution, since counterfeit AirPods can look convincing. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.






How we choose AirPods deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. Our Best AirPods guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the best choice for everyone: fit, listening habits, and the features you need all matter.
For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our roundups of the best Mac deals, iPad deals, and Apple Watch deals.

Black Friday is a great time to buy an iPad, with discounts spanning affordable everyday tablets, powerful Pro models, and clearance stock from previous generations. This year’s standout Black Friday iPad deal so far is on Apple’s newest tablet. Amazon has listed the 128GB iPad mini (A20 Pro) for $599 in the U.S., $100 off. 
For most people, we’d recommend the 11-inch M4 iPad Air. Amazon has listed the 128GB Wi-Fi model for $649 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., saving $100 and £80, respectively. If you mainly want an iPad for browsing, streaming, or schoolwork, the 128GB A16 iPad at $379 is the cheaper U.S. option. It’s $20 below its October Prime Day price, although it still costs $30 more than it did before Apple raised prices in June. 
The biggest savings are on configurations with more storage. Amazon has listed the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 1TB for $1,499 in the U.S. a saving of about $300. In the U.K. AO has the 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro for £300 off. Those are worth a look if you need the extra space. If you don’t, a lower-capacity model may still cost less. For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our Apple Black Friday deals roundups of the best Mac deals, Apple Watch deals and AirPods deals.
From November 27 to 30, Apple will include a $100/£80 Apple Gift Card when you buy an 11-inch or 13-inch M4 iPad Air directly from Apple, or a $125/£100 Apple Gift Card with an 11-inch or 13-inch M5 iPad Pro. The standard A16 iPad and iPad mini are excluded. Apple is also offering a $25/£20 gift card with eligible purchases of the Apple Pencil Pro or a Magic Keyboard for the iPad Air or iPad Pro. The gift card is for a future purchase. See our full guide to Apple’s Black Friday offer.
Which iPad should you buy this Black Friday?


M4 iPad Air – Our best all-round choice

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Air offers a strong balance of performance, screen size, and price without the premium cost of the Pro. The 11-inch model suits buyers who prioritize portability, while the 13-inch version gives you more room for multitasking and creative work.
A good Black Friday discount could make either size an attractive purchase. Compare storage capacities carefully, though: a larger advertised saving on a high-capacity model isn’t necessarily better value if you don’t need the extra space. 
U.S. Black Friday price: At Amazon, you can already get a saving of $100 off some iPad Air models, although in some cases these are selling out, in which case we are seeing Best Buy match the $100 off.  
U.K. Black Friday price: Amazon has £80 to £109 off the iPad Air configurations. For example, you can get the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB for £669, down from the usual £749. These are reasonable savings, although we saw better discounts during October Prime Day, with up to £144 off. Last Black Friday, selected M3 Air configurations received £100 discounts.
Apple’s deal: You can get a $100/£80 Apple Gift Card when you buy an 11-inch or 13-inch M4 iPad Air from Apple, which is similar to the Amazon U.K. deal. 






iPad Pro – Best for demanding creative work

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Pro is the option for buyers who need Apple’s highest-end tablet performance and premium display. It comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, but its capabilities – and price – will exceed what many people need for browsing, streaming, and everyday apps.
We’d look for a substantial saving rather than buy simply because it’s the most powerful iPad. Compare discounted M4 iPad Pro models, too: an older Pro could offer better value if its price is sufficiently below the equivalent M5 configuration. 
U.S. Black Friday price:  During October Prime Day, the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 256GB was $1,099, saving $100. So far we’re seeing nearly $300 off a 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro.
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought little to recommend on the M5 iPad Pro, with reductions of around £12. Last Black Friday, older M4 iPad Pro offers included a saving of up to £200. AO is selling the 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro for £1,649. 
Apple’s deal: You can get a $125/£100 Apple Gift Card with an 11-inch or 13-inch M5 iPad Pro.






iPad (A16) – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Apple




The A16 iPad remains a capable option for browsing, streaming, schoolwork, and everyday use. However, Apple raised its starting price by $100/£100 in June, and it doesn’t support Apple Intelligence.
That makes the final purchase price particularly important. A modest discount from today’s higher asking price may still leave you paying more than this iPad previously cost. With a replacement expected early in 2027, we’d look for a substantial Black Friday saving and compare the price with discounted iPad Air models before buying.
U.S. Black Friday price: This Black Friday, we are seeing $70 off the 128GB iPad. The current $379 price is lower than October’s $399 price. The 512GB iPad is £100 off at Amazon.
U.K. Black Friday price: October coverage listed the 256GB model at £499.97, around £29 off. Last Black Friday, the 128GB version was £299 and the 256GB version was £399. We hope to see even lower prices this year, but so far Amazon has the 128GB model for £399 and the 256GB model for £499, both £30 off. 






iPad mini with A20 Pro – Best for portability

				
					

				
			
Apple




The new iPad mini went on sale on November 6, replacing the A17 Pro model. It brings an 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter design, making it the option to consider if you want a compact iPad with the latest hardware.
Because it has only just arrived, we’d expect initial discounts to be smaller than clearance savings on its predecessor. The older A17 Pro mini could still be worthwhile at a sufficiently low price, but compare the saving with what you give up – particularly the new display.
U.S. Black Friday price: The A20 Pro mini wasn’t available during October Prime Day or last Black Friday. Amazon has it for $599, $100 off and the best price we’ve seen so far. Should you buy an iPad now or wait for a better deal?

				
					

				
			
There’s an iPad for everyone.

Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an iPad immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if the price is competitive. Compare the exact generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity rather than waiting for Black Friday simply because a larger discount might appear.
If you’re buying an iPad Air and already plan to buy an Apple Pencil or keyboard later, Apple’s gift card may be worth waiting for. For the iPad Pro, check retailer prices first. The 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 1TB has been listed at $299.01 off in the U.S. and £150 off in the U.K. at Amazon, both bigger savings than the Apple Gift Card.
Previous selling prices are particularly important this year because Apple raised iPad prices in June. During October Prime Day, the 128GB A16 iPad was $399, while the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB was $649. Both were discounted against Apple’s increased prices, but cost more than their regular prices before June. A saving from today’s asking price doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting an exceptional bargain.
For the M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro, we’d focus on finding a good price: We don’t expect replacements until 2027, as explained in our guide to the best time to buy an iPad. We’d be more cautious about the A16 iPad, which lacks Apple Intelligence and is expected to be replaced. Unless you find a substantial saving, waiting could get you a more capable entry-level model.
The new A20 Pro iPad mini has already seen price drops. In the U.S., the 128GB iPad mini (A20 Pro) is already down to $599, $100 off its $699 MSRP. That’s the deal we’d pick if you want the latest model. The older128GB iPad mini (A17 Pro) is $499 if you’d rather save another $100. In the U.K., the new iPad mini still starts at its full £699 price, so if you’re buying for the discount, we’d wait.






Should you buy an older iPad? 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older iPad can be a good buy if its price reflects its age and the features you give up. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of its replacement, matching screen size, storage, and connectivity where possible. A large saving from an old launch price doesn’t necessarily make it better value.
The M3 iPad Air and M4 iPad Pro are worth considering at substantial clearance discounts. Both remain capable options, and you may get more benefit from a lower price or additional storage than from the latest processor. However, if the newer equivalent costs only slightly more, the saving may not justify choosing the older generation.
The A17 Pro iPad mini also deserves consideration now that the A20 Pro model has arrived. It supports Apple Intelligence and remains a capable compact tablet, but you miss the newer model’s OLED display, faster processor, and thinner, lighter design. We’d want a meaningful saving rather than a small reduction from its former asking price.
Be more cautious with much older models. Check whether they support the current version of iPadOS and the apps and features you need. Compatibility today doesn’t guarantee how many future software upgrades they’ll receive. Apple Intelligence support also varies: don’t assume every older Air, Pro, or mini includes it.
If you already own an Apple Pencil or keyboard, check compatibility before changing generations. Keeping compatible accessories could make an older iPad better value, while replacing them could erase part of your saving. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges.






iPad deals to avoid
Check the exact configuration before comparing offers. Retailer listings can emphasize iPad, Air, or Pro without making the generation obvious. Confirm the chip, screen size, storage capacity, and whether you’re buying Wi-Fi or Wi-Fi + Cellular. A cheaper listing may be a different model rather than a better deal.
Don’t let a large advertised discount tempt you into paying for storage or connectivity you won’t use. A heavily reduced high-capacity or cellular iPad can still cost more than a simpler configuration that meets your needs. Compare the final purchase prices, rather than assuming the biggest saving represents the best value.
Check whether the price includes nano-texture glass, too. This optional finish (on the 1TB and 2TB M5 iPad Pro and the 256GB and 512GB A20 Pro iPad mini) reduces glare and makes fingerprints and oily smudges less noticeable, which can be useful if reflections make your iPad difficult to see in bright rooms or outdoors. It avoids much of the washed-out appearance associated with ordinary matte finishes, but contrast can drop at some viewing angles and the surface may be more scratch-sensitive. Availability depends on the model and storage configuration, so you could end up paying for both the finish and additional storage. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may be better value. Read our guide to nano-texture glass and whether you need it.
Our iPad buying guide considers cellular a luxury for most buyers. If you mainly use your iPad somewhere with Wi-Fi, you may get little benefit from the extra hardware. For occasional use elsewhere, sharing your iPhone’s connection through Personal Hotspot can be a more economical option.
Cellular makes more sense if you regularly need an independent connection while commuting or traveling; it also adds built-in GPS for accurate location tracking. Factor in any data-plan charges and compare the total cost of a contract with buying outright. A cellular model can still be worthwhile if its sale price matches or beats the equivalent Wi-Fi version—you don’t have to activate a data plan simply because the hardware is included.
Judge savings against previous selling prices as well as Apple’s current price. Following June’s price increases, a discounted iPad may still cost more than it did earlier in the year. Also distinguish a cash discount from a gift-card offer: a gift card doesn’t reduce the amount you pay for the iPad and is useful only if you’ll spend it.
Check what any bundle includes. A keyboard, case, or stylus doesn’t automatically make an offer better value, particularly if the accessories aren’t the versions you want. Read the conditions attached to “free” iPads, trade-in promotions, contracts, and rebates before comparing their total cost with buying outright.
Finally, check whether the iPad is new, refurbished, or used, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For used or refurbished models, look for information about battery condition and confirm that Activation Lock has been removed. Be cautious about devices that remain tied to a previous owner or an organization’s management system.






How we choose iPad deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on iPad reviews and everyday use. We consider performance, display quality, portability, battery life, and accessory support alongside price to explain which iPads suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess whether paying more brings practical benefits. title: Apple Still Working on Giant Foldable iPad That Could Cost $5,000
content:
Apple is still developing a large foldable iPad despite ongoing technical challenges and uncertainty about whether it will ever launch, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Speaking on the latest episode of the "Power On" podcast, Gurman revived discussion about the device, known internally as "Project J312." He described it as a foldable iPad with a display measuring around 19 to 20 inches, saying it would resemble a "gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside." The device could cost between $3,000 and $5,000.

Apple apparently originally wanted to announce the device by 2027, before pushing that target to 2028. The timeframe has since slipped to around 2029, although Gurman cautioned that it remains uncertain whether the product will ever reach the market.

Gurman cited cost and display manufacturing yield issues among the obstacles facing development, along with concerns that the ‌iPad‌ could be cumbersome. Apple has also yet to determine which operating system it would run, with macOS, iPadOS, and an entirely new platform all remaining possibilities. Gurman described the unresolved software direction as another complication, but expressed excitement about the device's potential.

report from research firm Omdia in September, which claimed that Apple had canceled plans for a foldable MacBook measuring between 16.1 and 18 inches when unfolded. Earlier reports had described that device as a large-screened foldable ‌iPad‌, although it remains unclear whether Omdia was referring to the same project Gurman discussed.

discussed the foldable ‌iPad‌ in April, describing it as a priority for John Ternus while warning that it could remain an unreleased experiment. The potential 2029 timeframe was already part of Gurman's report from October 2025, when weight and display technology issues were said to threaten Apple's earlier 2028 target.

Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?


Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.

Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.
It’s more watch than most people need. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.

Apple

Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.
U.S. We’d buy now at the prices we are seeing for Black Friday. Amazon has the Apple Watch Series 12 GPS for $299 in 42mm and $349 in 46mm, down from $349 and $399 during October Prime Day. The SE 3 GPS is $179 in 40mm and $209 in 44mm, down from $199 and $229 in October. The Ultra 4 is $699, $75 below its October Prime Day price of $774.
U.K. Amazon’s £199 price for the 40mm Apple Watch SE 3 GPS matches its October Prime Day deal. The 44mm model is £223, £6 below its October price of £229. If you want the larger screen, it’s £24 more than the 40mm model at these prices.
Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.






Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.
Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.
The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.






Apple Watch deals to avoid 

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.
Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Our GPS versus cellular Apple Watch guide explains the trade-offs.
Check the rest of the configuration, too. A premium case material or expensive band can make a heavily discounted watch cost more than a simpler version that meets your needs. Judge offers against previous selling prices as well as the advertised reduction: a large saving from the original launch price doesn’t necessarily mean exceptional value. Check any spending requirements, contracts, trade-ins, or rebates attached to offers advertising a “free” Apple Watch.
Finally, check whether you’re buying a new, refurbished, or used watch, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For a used or refurbished model, check the stated battery condition and confirm that it has been removed from the previous owner’s account, with Activation Lock turned off. Make sure the watch is compatible with your iPhone before ordering.






How we choose Apple Watch deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on Apple Watch reviews and everyday wear. We consider comfort, performance, battery life, charging, health and fitness features, and value – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our Series 12 review assessed battery life and charging performance alongside its newer health features. We also draw on everyday experience: our cellular Apple Watch testing examines whether staying connected without an iPhone justified the extra hardware and subscription costs.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. We check the generation, case size, material, connectivity, and included band so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside discounted replacements.
Our Best Apple Watch guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the right choice: your budget, wrist size, activities, and the features you need all matter.

title: Did Apple just save the iPhone Duo?
content:
Macworld





The tech industry is obsessed with change, but most customers feel much more ambivalent about the concept. The announcement of a tweak to Facebook’s algorithm or Netflix’s interface is rarely the cause of celebration: “Why did they change it?” is the motto of casual tech users across the planet. And when it comes to hardware, the world can be divided into a tiny minority of novelty seekers, and a vast majority who just want a product that does the same as the last generation in a new color and with fewer bugs.
The iPhone Duo is designed to appeal to the first demographic far more than the second, which is why it will struggle to achieve mainstream appeal. It is, by the standards of iPhones at any rate, remarkably different from its predecessors, and I don’t mean that as a compliment. It’s aggressively, confrontationally new, and the word that keeps occurring to me is “difficult.”
I’ve been using one as my primary device for a month. I’d never claim to be a fast learner, but by this point in the testing cycle I’m generally up to speed. (Switching from the Home button on the iPhone 8 to the upward swipe on the iPhone XS, for example, felt natural within days.) That isn’t the case with the Duo. The folding and unfolding process still doesn’t come naturally; I haven’t found a comfortable way to hold it when open and in landscape orientation; it’s more difficult to jump up to the top of webpages and to summon the Control Center; and my brain is yet to fully take on board the shift of many interface elements from the bottom or top to the side of the screen.
The onboarding speed bump that’s caused me the most annoyance, however, is Touch ID. This is surprising, because I would consider myself a fan of that technology. When Touch ID began its transition to Face ID way back in 2017, I was in the “Why did they change it?” crowd. Touch ID was reliable, and not noticeably slow. Face ID sometimes went wrong and was not appreciably more convenient. I recognized that the change allowed Apple to ditch the Home button and claw back more screen space, but facial recognition itself struck me then as a means to an end rather than a positive evolution of the user experience.

				
					

				
			Where’s the Touch ID sensor? It’s on the right. This time.

Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




However, my love of Touch ID is because the conventional iPhone design suits Touch ID. With other devices and in other contexts, it’s not quite as convenient. Such is the case with my 5th-gen iPad Air, which sits most of the time on a stand next to my MacBook with its power button awkwardly placed slightly behind the laptop. Any time I have to log in, I’m reminded of how much easier life would be if the iPad Air had Face ID, and I sometimes even look up prices of second-hand iPad Pros. Or the MacBook Pro itself, which has a raised-up stand of its own and therefore forces me to reach up to access its in-keyboard fingerprint sensor, evoking similar reservations to those I have about touchscreen laptops.
The iPhone Duo is the worst of all. It’s a nightmare for accessing the Touch ID sensor precisely because of its formal versatility. If it’s closed and in portrait orientation, or open and landscape, the sensor is two-thirds of the way up the right-hand edge (where no such sensor has ever previously been on an Apple product, as far as I’m aware), so realistically you have to use your right index finger. But it doesn’t feel natural, and certainly isn’t comfortable. When closed, you can just about reach behind the phone and use your left index fingertip, but the angle makes it very unreliable.
The opposite two modes, closed in landscape and open in portrait, put the sensor partway along the top edge. Both are inconvenient, but in subtly different ways. For closed/landscape, when you hold it a little like a game controller, the left index can reach up without moving the hand, although the angle is suboptimal. For open/portrait, your hands most likely sit at the lower end to avoid the camera module, so you have to reach upwards, and the right index is probably your best choice.
Now, I worry that the preceding two paragraphs may have strained the reader’s patience. But such is the experience of using Touch ID on the iPhone Duo: tedious and complicated. It’s essential to record at least two fingerprints (you may also want to include your right thumb for occasional use in open/landscape), and the methods of accessing the sensor vary so much from each other and from what’s come before that you have no hope of depending on, or building, muscle memory. Add in the fact that, unlike the Home button, the power button is not visible from the front of the device, and it becomes clear why Apple feels it necessary to add on-screen indicators to help you find the sensor.

				
					

				
			Setting up Unlock with Front Camera is easy, and well worth doing.
David Price / Foundry




My dissatisfaction with all this turned to delight, however, when Apple found a way to achieve the impossible and retrospectively add a hardware feature to an already released product. Well, sort of. The iPhone Duo is obviously not getting Face ID, because the necessary sensors are not there. But it’s getting the next best thing. As of the second beta of iOS 27.3, the Duo gets a new feature called Unlock with Front Camera that was borrowed from HomeView. I explain how to get this in a separate article, but I’ll tell you here: It’s a game-changer.
Facial unlock doesn’t have the same access privileges as Face ID, because it depends on sensors that aren’t as sophisticated and cannot offer the same level of security. Quite a lot of the time, including sensitive app unlocks, the Duo will insist that you use the more secure Touch ID instead (or enter your passcode). But many phone unlocks can now be performed by looking at the front camera, and a glance can also uncover details of previously hidden notifications. For removing a large number of small pain points, and for making a difficult device significantly less difficult, Apple deserves tremendous praise.

content:
Apple is facing a formal probe in South Korea over allegations that its iPhone 16 advertising misled consumers about the availability of Apple Intelligence features.


Investigators at the country's Fair Trade Commission (FTC) have referred Apple and Apple Korea for review, alleging that several Apple Intelligence features were not delivered as advertised, including Genmoji, Image Playground, and Siri's ability to understand personal context and onscreen awareness.

The allegations focus on whether Apple adequately explained which features were available and when others would arrive. For example, the FTC's report notes that Siri's personal-context capabilities were advertised for Korean availability in early April 2025 but did not arrive until October 2026, approximately 18 months later.

Apple provided MacRumors with the following statement:
"At Apple, we deeply value the relationship with our customers in Korea and have always focused on delivering the best products and services in the world. Since we added Korean language support for Apple Intelligence last year, users have benefited from dozens of powerful features that are integrated across Apple's platforms. And we have continued to build on that commitment with the recent launch of Korean language support for Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that's more capable, conversational, and personal. We have cooperated with the KFTC's investigation and disagree with the conclusions in the Examiner's Report. We look forward to presenting a fulsome defense before the Commission."
The Commission has yet to issue a final ruling or impose a penalty.

removed its "available now" marketing claim on its Apple Intelligence page, following a National Advertising Division inquiry. The advertising watchdog found that the wording implied that all listed features were available, and that a footnote explaining the phased rollout was insufficiently clear. Apple disagreed with the findings but ultimately complied with the recommendation.

$250 million settlement in May 2026 over a U.S. class-action lawsuit alleging it misled buyers about the availability of Apple Intelligence and Siri features when the iPhone 16 was released in September 2024.

Original article updated with Apple's statement.

The monitor might be the second-most important part of your Mac’s setup after the Mac, of course–you can’t use any desktop computer without one and even the 16-inch screen on the MacBook Pro feels cramped if you are having a particularly productive morning. Spread your work out by plugging in multiple monitors to your Mac and extending your desktop over a wider space.
Because you’ll spend a lot of time looking at the display, you’ll want to invest wisely. Not only will you want a monitor that provides a pleasing experience, but the quality of the images on the screen can also affect your work.
However, picking a new monitor can be daunting. Not only are there many manufacturers to choose from, but there are also lots of sizes, resolutions, and features to consider—and when we say lots, we mean lots. We’re here to help guide you while you shop, and we have some tips on what to look for in a monitor plus advice on how many monitors each Mac can handle.
Best Mac monitors 2026

The MA270U/P can connect to a Mac through HDMI or USB-C. The USB-C connection offers 90 watts of power so it can charge your MacBook at the same time. It offers image quality that could satisfy users in a production environment–that’s one way of saying that its quality is better than what general users usually get. You might be able to find a 27-inch 4K display that’s a little cheaper, but it won’t look this good.–Roman Loyola

As a production display, the Studio Display is still expensive but looks affordable compared to the Apple Studio Display XDR. Buyers will enjoy its handsome design, good image quality, and impressive spatial audio, but you can save a lot of money by going with a non-Apple display.
Apple displays have always produced very good image quality, and the Studio Display continues that tradition. Colors are rich, contrast is good, and the brightness is suitable for most tasks.
The Studio Display has a tilt-adjustable stand, but it does not pivot between landscape and portrait modes—a WESA mount beings you a portrait option with the right monitor arm or stand. You can get a stand that provides about four inches of height adjustment but it doesn’t come cheap. The price tag for the tilt- and height-adjustable stand is a whopping $400/£400 more. That Apple stand on its own is about half the price of a comparable third-party 5K monitor with its own height-adjustable stand, such as the BenQ MA270S, reviewed below.
The Studio Display has six speakers (four force-canceling woofers, and two high-performance tweeters) that sound better than most displays we’ve used but are no match for a decent independent speaker.
There’s nothing wrong with this display. Brightness uniformity is good, and color accuracy is excellent. It’s just an old panel, with poor motion clarity from a slow pixel response and a complete lack of modern expected display properties. It’s 2026, and all but the very cheapest monitors have refresh rates over 60Hz, adaptive refresh, HDR, or all of the above.
For a monitor being sold new in 2026, the Studio Display looks like what a nice $999 5K display should. Apple’s Studio Display and Pro Display are seriously expensive, and they’re very much designed for professional and creative users who need 5K or 6K displays for graphics and video work. Not everyone needs such a high-res display though, and I’ve always found that a QHD (quad-HD) display with 2,560×1,440 resolution is the affordable sweet spot that works well for both general office work and off-duty entertainment. HP’s somewhat clumsily named E27u G4 is a good option here, providing an attractive QHD display with a variety of connectivity features for just $424/£286.80.
You’re not going to get a top-of-the-range display for that price, and the E27u does lack a few added extras, such as a built-in webcam or speakers. It gets all the basics right, though, with good image quality, multiple video inputs, and a useful built-in USB hub. The display’s 250 nits brightness may be relatively modest, but we found that the E27u looks bright and sharp enough for working with productivity software such as Microsoft Office, and also for streaming video from the BBC iPlayer and Apple TV+. And while Apple charges an extra £400 for an upgrade that allows you to adjust the height of its Studio Display—which is more than the entire cost of the E27u—you can tilt, swivel and adjust the height of the E27u, and even rotate it into upright (portrait) mode at no extra cost.
The E27u includes HDMI, DisplayPort and USB-C interfaces for connecting to your Mac, with the USB-C port also providing 65W power to charge a MacBook or other laptop if required. When using the USB-C connection you can also use four USB-A ports to connect devices such a keyboard, mouse or hard drive, and there’s also a second DisplayPort interface that will allow you to daisy-chain a second monitor if required. Our only complaint is that there’s no audio connector that would allow you to connect headphones or a set of external speakers to the display – although HP does sell a special ‘speaker bar’ that bolts onto the bottom of the screen if you want to add audio ($43.00/£40.00).–Cliff Joseph
How we test monitors
Macworld staff and other contributors with decades of combined experience have tested the displays in this round up. 
We thoroughly test each monitor, evaluating clarity of the image, maximum brightness, contrast ratio, and color accuracy and color gamut and other aspects of image quality. Motion clarity is also important, especially if the monitor will be used for gaming or other graphical applications.  
We also look at the build quality as well as usability and connectivity, and any special features or modes on offer, especially any that require software that may, or may not work as expected on a Mac. 
Why you should trust Macworld
Macworld prides itself on our experience and expertise when it comes to all things Mac. We conduct in-depth reviews of numerous monitors annually. Our comprehensive recommendations undergo rigorous testing and evaluation by our expert reviewers, who adhere to both performance benchmarks and stringent usability standards.
Should I buy an Apple display for my Mac?
Apple sells displays for its Macs, and you could go with its offerings, which are included above, but its displays are a quite bit more expensive than what third parties offer. 
Buying from a different company may mean you may not get a feature that Apple offers, but it may also be a feature that you don’t need, depending on how you use the monitor. 
There are plenty of companies that have great monitors that you can use with your Mac, without having to take out a second mortgage. Our sister publication PCWorld has tested several displays, and we list their top-rated ones that we have been able to confirm work with Macs, alongside the monitors we have reviewed below. Here are our recommendations in order, starting with Apple’s most expensive.
Are there compatibility issues for Mac monitors?
There are compatibility issues for plain M1, M2 and M3 Macs, which, unlike M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max/Ultra MacBooks, can’t natively connect to more than one external display. Fortunately, there is a solution and we show you how to connect multiple monitors to M1, M2 and M3 Macs in a separate article.
How to choose a Mac monitor
Display technology is a bit of a movable feast, with a lot of confusing jargon and technical features to wade through, as well as a variety of different interfaces and cables that are used by Apple itself and the various monitor manufacturers. So it’s worth taking a closer look at some of the factors that you need to think about when buying a monitor for your Mac.
Screen size
Size isn’t everything, as the saying goes, but it’s a good place to start. Your decision will be influenced by how much desk space you have, and how comfortable you are while using the display. Some people think that a big screen is best, but then when they start to use it daily, they find that it’s too big. And the same goes for customers who think a small screen is best.
If you’re looking for a size to start with for your own personal research, we recommend 24 inches—just like with Apple’s iMac. That seems like a good size for most people, and it’s easy to go up or down from that point. Most people tend to go between 24 and 27 inches for home use.
For professionals—graphics, video, audio, even spreadsheets—a large screen will help you be more productive. Think 27 inches and higher. You’ll be able to fit more elements on the screen and not waste your time scrolling.
If on-screen real estate is valuable to you, consider a multi-display setup. A smaller screen can be used for things like chat, email, web, and more, while the bigger screen is your main workspace. Or get screens of the same size and maximize the space.
Screen resolution
Screen resolution can go hand-in-hand with screen size. Screen resolution refers to the number of pixels used to create what you see on the screen. The higher the resolution, the more detail you can see. Larger displays tend to have more resolution options, as well as the ability to support higher resolutions.
Often, when you find two displays that are the same size but have a wide price difference, it’s mostly because of the screen resolution. Monitors with high resolutions are more expensive. For example, Apple’s $1,599 Studio Display is 27 inches, and it has a high screen resolution of 5120×2880 (5K resolution). On the other hand, LG sells the 27-inch 27UK650-W, but it’s a 3840×2160 (4K) resolution display for content creators, and it’s $350–lower resolution, but $1,249 cheaper. (There actually aren’t other 27-inch 5K monitors available, except for the $1,449 LG UltraFine 27MD5KL-B.)
So what screen resolution should you get? Here are some suggestions; these are guidelines that you can adjust based on your preferences.
For general purpose use, such as web browsing, email, media viewing, small photo and video projects and viewing: 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 (HD)
For more-involved content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 3840×2160 (4K)
For pro-level content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 4K or higher
Want to use an 8K monitor? Read How to connect an 8K display to your Mac.
Connecting a monitor to a Mac
How a monitor connects to a Mac can be confusing. The traditional HDMI and DisplayPort connectors used by many monitors are being replaced–or complemented–by USB-C and Thunderbolt ports. And though USB-C and Thunderbolt cables may look the same, there are actually some important technical differences between them, so it’s important to check which ports your new monitor uses and make sure you buy the correct cables and adapters.
Most recent Mac models have Thunderbolt ports, so if you buy a monitor that has HDMI or DisplayPort interfaces only, then you’ll need an adapter to connect to the Mac. This can get a bit confusing, but Apple does provide a list of the ports included on most recent Mac models so that you can figure out what you need.
Apple also provides a guide to HDMI and DisplayPort technology, which covers Mac models going right back to 2008, so that should provide all the info you need for all the Macs you use at home or at work. Less expensive monitors still tend to use HDMI and DisplayPort, and while it’s not too costly to buy adapters that will allow you to connect your Mac, we reckon it’s worth future-proofing your new monitor by getting one that includes at least one USB-C or Thunderbolt port.
If a display uses Thunderbolt to connect to the Mac, it may have additional USB-C or Thunderbolt ports so the display can act as a hub. In this case, If you have a device you want to connect to your Mac, you can connect it to one of the ports on the monitor, which is already connected to the Mac and probably in an easier location for access.  
Look for a USB-C or Thunderbolt connection with power delivery (PD) that can charge your MacBook. A 65W PD will be enough for a MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro, but you’ll need at least 90W for a 15-inch or 16-inch Pro.
Read our article on how to connect a second screen to a Mac which explains everything you need to know about how to identify which ports you have, the adapters you will require, and how to set things up.
Ergonomics
If you’re going to spend a lot of time sitting at a desk looking at your lovely new display then you need to keep ergonomics in mind. The ability to tilt the angle of the monitor back and forth, swivel it around for easy viewing, and adjust the height of the monitor in order to avoid an aching back or neck.
Some monitors can pivot or rotate in either landscape or portrait mode.
As a rough guide, there is a point at about 2 to 3 inches from the top of the screen that should be at eye level. Obviously, eye level varies from one person to another, so it’s important that you can adjust the screen for your own personal comfort. You may also prefer a monitor that doesn’t suffer from glare, or you will be forever repositioning the monitor (or your head) to compensate for that.
Other considerations
There are other considerations you’ll want to make when shopping for a monitor. A lot of these come down to personal preference or what you need for the work you do. They include:
Color space (gamut): The number of colors a monitor can show. Professionals need specific color spaces.
Refresh rate: The frequency when a screen is refreshed. Higher rates produce smoother animations.
Webcam: Some displays have a built-in camera you can use for FaceTime and other video conferencing apps, or to record yourself.
Speakers: If you plan on frequently viewing or listening to media, a good set of speakers makes for a better experience.
How many monitors does my Mac allow?
The number of external displays you can hook up to your Mac, depends on its M-series processor. In short, any Pro or Max M1 to M5 processor supports at least two monitors, but base M1/M2/M3 and Neo MacBooks might be limited to just one. See below for the full list and also a link to our tutorial about how to get round the limitations.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M1 or M2 chip, or is the MacBook Neo, it is limited to using just one external monitor unless you follow our DisplayLink workaround tutorial.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M3 chip, it can only use two external monitors if its own lid is closed (so not showing its own screen) unless you follow our tips in the link above.
• If your Mac has a base M4/M5, M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip, it is limited to using two external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Pro chip, it is limited to using three external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Max chip, it is limited to using four external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

Comment Corner 
I thought the community was a good self- help part of Apple. A way to find out if others had similar issues, or if any workarounds or solutions were found. I would have thought even Apple people could get a feel for any trends in potential issues or feedback. Sure, there were people just ranting or expecting a direct connection with Apple. But the trend to just disconnect from users of your products just seems misguided.
John S. via email 





Isn’t it possible that closing the forum is an attempt to get people to try and use Apple Intelligence to fix their problems either so that it racks up usage and eventually they can charge people, or so the Apple LLM can build up its knowledge base and become the defacto AI source of information on Apple products and tech support for those products? 
 Jesse R. via email 





Since no new posts were allowed, I called the support number and I think I found out why they are closing the forums. They have instituted an AI system that walks you through solving your problem. It was very adaptive and the voice was pleasant. There were even background voices! Alas, it couldn’t solve my problem so I was connected to a real person. However, it seems that Apple is entrusting it’s support to AI rather than users. 
Gary B. via email 





I really hated to see this, as I have good memories of participating there often back in the early 2000s, when it really was more of a community. There were lots of really helpful and knowledgeable people, and often a real sense of camaraderie. 
As time went along, it did get less and less useful. I think a big part of it was Apple’s reorganization of the forum. It became hard to navigate to a particular area, like a section devoted to one particular Mac, one OS, one app, etc., where regulars who knew about that topic tended to hang out.  In addition to that, just the sheer growth of Apple and the massive amount of traffic, a lot from one-time users, made it really not possible to have the same kind of close-knit community anymore. 
And, admittedly, there are all kinds of alternatives now that are better options; but I guess I just have nostalgia for what it once was. I had a lot of good times and learned a lot there.  
Donnie A. via email

I am so happy to hear THE END of this mostly useless platform thanks to the Self-described Experts and Gurus who gave me mostly Snarky Replies and Condescending solutions to my Mac’s problems like, “Get A New Mac!” What a bunch of Pompous Asses!!! USB-C is the modern connection standard shared by most new devices today. It comes in several different formats—USB-C, USB4 and Thunderbolt—but they all have the same reversible connector at the end and are interchangeable and backwards compatible. All of Apple’s new devices now use USB-C or Thunderbolt for charging and data transfers.
Some cables are only really good for charging as their data-transfer (bandwidth) rate is too slow to be practical. In the reviews below we note both charging power (measured in watts) and data-transfer rate—measured in either megabits per second (Mbps) or gigabits per second (Gbps). If you are connecting the cable to a monitor, storage device, hub or docking station the minimum data speed should be 5Gbps but go higher if you can. If you just want to use it for charging an iPhone, iPad or MacBook, the data speed matters less.
We’ve tried and tested the best USB-C and Thunderbolt cables here. If you want to jump straight to our recommendations click the one that meets your requirements:
Best USB-C cable for iPhone and iPad
Best USB-C cable for Mac
Best Thunderbolt 5 cables
Best Thunderbolt 4 cables
You can find cheaper online but we recommend cables only from trusted brands, such as Anker, Apple, Beats, Belkin, Cable Matters, CalDigit, Native Union, Plugable, and Ugreen. When charging your precious devices, you want to be sure that you aren’t putting them at risk of overheating and potentially causing a fire in your home.
Apple’s old Lightning connector was also reversible—where it doesn’t matter which side of the connector faces up or down as you plug it in—so no big change there, but USB-C is much more than just a symmetrical design. It can transfer data much faster—pushing Lightning’s 0.48Gbps to up to 120Gbps, a 24,900% speed increase.
Apple’s iPhone 15 and newer have a USB-C port, replacing the old trusty but proprietary Lightning cable that has been a part of iPhones and older iPads since 2012. Apple supplies a USB-C charging cable in the box, but if you want a single cable for fast charging and data transfers—or just a spare charging cable—we’ve rounded up some of our favorites to help you get the best one.
Some are fast, some are super-powerful, some are both, a few are retractable, and some are just fun. Yes… fun!
We go into more detail about everything you need to know about USB-C cables after the chart of best cables, but for now you need to know about the cable of your dreams:
Which speed (measured in watts) your devices require: an iPhone needs at least 20W to fast-charge, an iPad 30W, a MacBook Air at least 70W, a MacBook Pro 100W and the 16-inch Pro 140W. While the MacBook Neo doesn’t officially support fast charging, a 30W charger will speed things up but any higher won’t likely do much more for that laptop model.
Do you need it to transfer data as well as supply power? Most charging cables are limited to a rather slow 480Mbps data rate. If you want proper bandwidth as well as charging power look for at least 5Gbps or as much as 80Gbps.
How long should it be: if the charger is within arms reach of your device a short cable might suffice where a long cable will just be an inconvenience, but if you want to charge your iPhone, Pad or MacBook while sat on the sofa a longer cable will make all the difference.
We’ve supplied the cable data to these questions in our reviews below.
The difference between USB-A, Lightning, USB-C, and Thunderbolt

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Thunderbolt looks identical to USB-C and uses the same connector, but is much faster. Thunderbolt 3 and 4 can reach 40Gbps, and Thunderbolt 5 stretches as far as 80Gbps (and even 120Gbps unidirectionally).
Note that the cables reviewed here are USB-C to USB-C (or backwards-compatible Thunderbolt to Thunderbolt). Old iPhone chargers had the non-reversible rectangular USB-A connector to connect to the charger and a Lightning connector that went into the iPhone. Don’t stick with legacy USB-A at one end as the old standard is limited in data transfer speed to 10Gbps and pegged back in charging speed to just a rather pathetic 15W.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Using a USB-C charger will enable fast charging even for iPhones with a Lightning port. You can still charge an Apple device with a USB-A charger but not at the fastest speed. From the iPhone 15 onwards it’s USB-C into the charger and USB-C into the iPhone. See our roundup of the best USB-C chargers for iPhone.
We have even more tips that show you the fastest ways to charge an iPhone.
Best USB-C cables for iPhone and iPad
Elsewhere we have rounded up the best Lightning cables we’ve seen for iPhones older than the iPhone 15. USB-A is the larger, non-reversible connector. USB-C is required for iPhone fast charging.
From the iPhone 15 onwards—also from the AirPods Pro 2—you’ll need a cable with USB-C on both ends (USB-C-to-USB-C) to charge an iPhone or iPad unless you charge wirelessly: check out the best MagSafe wireless iPhone chargers.
All iPads on sale today feature a USB-C connector. But even the 10th Gen iPad’s USB-C is still limited to a 480Mbps data speed. The iPad mini has a USB-C port that supports 5Gbps; the iPad Air 10Gbps; and the iPad Pro has a USB4/Thunderbolt port that can zip data along at 40Gbps. Check your iPad’s data transfer rate before choosing a new cable.
For charging only, any of the USB-C cables reviewed below will be fine as 20W should be enough to charge even an iPad. But if you are connecting to other devices or syncing via cable, we recommend cables that support faster data transfers. Best USB-C cables for Mac
Only the MacBook Neo uses standard USB-C. Other Macs since the 2016 MacBook Pro have much faster Thunderbolt ports: either Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5. Plain M1/M2 Macs (not Pro or Max) are listed as Thunderbolt/USB4 but can be regarded as the same as Thunderbolt 4 except for their one-screen limitation. Some of Apple’s latest Macs feature Thunderbolt 5, which has a potential data transfer rate of 80Gbps (120Gbps for video) and 240W charging power.
If you are buying today, we recommend you go for a Thunderbolt 4 or 5 cable, which are the most capable standards and fully backward compatible with Thunderbolt 3 and USB-C. But they’re pricey, and if speedy data transfer is not a priority or you require the cable for charging only, a slower USB-C cable will suffice for fast charging. MacBooks require cables and chargers that support the USB Power Delivery (PD) standard. PD 3.0 supports up to 100W. PD 3.1 goes up to 240W.

Thunderbolt  cables
Macs use the Thunderbolt standard that is faster and more capable than USB-C. If all you require the cable for is charging, then the relevant USB-C charging cable should be fine, but for anything requiring fast data transfers go for higher-bandwidth Thunderbolt. Thunderbolt cables are all certified to both speedy charging and very fast data-transfer speeds, whereas you need to check that the USB-C cables you think will do the job actually will—although buy from our recommendations above and you should be fine.
Standard copper “passive” Thunderbolt cables are also usually shorter as the data loses speed over longer distances. To get around this requires an “active” Thunderbolt cable that includes sophisticated chip engineering to push the signal along at the best speed, but you’ll see the price increase accordingly. Anything over 1m in length usually requires active technology.
Best Thunderbolt 5 cables
Thunderbolt 5 is superior to Thunderbolt 4 with doubled data/video bandwidth (80/120Gbps vs 40Gbps), improved PCIe 4.0 support (32Gbps vs 64Gbps), and enhanced power delivery (240W vs 100W). It’s backwards compatible all the way back to USB-C so—if you can afford it—it’s a more future-proof solution than Thunderbolt 3 or 4. Thunderbolt 5 transmits up to 80Gbps bidirectionally and 120Gbps in one direction with Bandwidth Boost enabled to support demanding display configurations.

Know your cables
Not all USB-C cables offer the same capabilities, so we explain each factor you need to consider. Fear not, for basic iPhone charging most USB-C cables will be fine. But some are finer than others. Macs use Thunderbolt cables that have the same Type-C connector as USB-C so look the same but have faster data transfer and charging speed options. You can use a Thunderbolt cable to charge USB-C devices, too.
Apple ships a USB-C Charge Cable with the newest iPhones but Mac users need to buy a Thunderbolt cable to connect to a docking station or fast storage device. Having a spare cable or two hanging around the house or office is always advisable—and there are better, cheaper, and more colorful USB-C and Thunderbolt cables than just those sold by Apple.
We’ve focused on USB-C charging cables as most people need them just to attach to a USB-C charger, but cables offer both charging and data transfers, although at different capabilities, depending on your requirements. 
Charging: All USB-C cables can carry a minimum of 60W (3A x 20V). Some support 100W (5A x 20V) charging, and some new Thunderbolt cables can charge at up to 240W. 60W is more than you need for a phone and is fine for the MacBook Neo and Air and 13-inch MacBook Pro. Go for at least a 100W cable for the 14-inch MacBook Pro. As Apple states 70W as the minimum for fast-charging the MacBook Air, a 100W cable is also recommended for these users. While 100W is fine for a 16-inch MacBook Pro, that model can be charged at up to 140W, although Apple restricts fast-charging for that model to its own $49/£49 USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable, which is included with all MacBooks.
iPhone 15-16 series: Apple says that the iPhone 15-16 can be fast-charged from zero to 50% in 30 minutes using at least a 20W USB-C power adapter, which is the same speed the iPhone 14 got via Lightning. Tests have shown that such iPhones can reach charging speeds of up to 30W so we think a 20W charger isn’t going to offer iPhone charging as fast as you can get. 
iPhone 17 series: Up to 50% charge in 20 minutes with 40W adapter or higher paired with USB‑C charging cable, and up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with 30W adapter or higher paired with MagSafe Charger.
iPhone 18 series: Up to a 50% charge in around 15 minutes when using 60W‑capable adapter or higher with Adjustable Voltage Supply paired with USB‑C charging cable, and up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with 35W adapter or higher paired with MagSafe Charger.
Check out our reviews of the best iPhone chargers.
Length: A long cable can be messy when your device is close to the charger, but a short one could leave your iPhone dangling out of reach. You may need different lengths of USB-C cable for each of your charging spaces. When it comes to transferring data, choose a cable that’s as short as you need as the longer the cable, the greater the risk of signal degradation—invest in a Thunderbolt 4 or 5 cable for 2m data-strength confidence. Or look at a coiled cable such as the Native Union POP Cable reviewed above.
Data transfer speed: iPhones with Lightning ports are limited to a slow USB 2.0 data transfer rate of just 480Mbps (480 megabits per second). Compare that to your Mac, whose Thunderbolt connection can reach up to 40Gbps on Thunderbolt 4 and 120Gbps on Thunderbolt 5—that’s 250 times faster! Data transfer speed doesn’t matter if all you are doing is charging a device but it is vital when connecting your Apple device to storage drives, docking stations, or monitors.
While the entry-level iPad is also limited to 480Mbps, the iPad Pro, like a MacBook, supports Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps maximum. The iPhone 15/16/17 and 15/16 Plus features USB-C that is limited to 480Mbps as with Lightning, but the iPhone 15/16/17/18 Pro and Pro Max’s USB-C can sync at 10Gbps—useful for backing up video or photos to a computer.
Note that the USB-C cable Apple supplies with the iPhone 15-18 families is a “Charge” cable and limited to 480Mbps for syncing. If you use the Pro or Pro Max model with a cable for data transfer, you’ll do better with a 10Gbps or higher bandwidth cable.





 FAQ 


1.
Which USB-C cable do I need to connect to a USB-C monitor
DisplayPort Alternate Mode is a feature available to USB-C and Thunderbolt that handles video as if the USB-C cable was a DisplayPort cable. USB-C monitors can therefore connect directly to your laptop or via a USB-C hub or USB-C or Thunderbolt dock.
However, not every USB-C cable supports video transfer so you need to choose the right type of cable.
If your external display supports a direct USB-C connection, look for a cable that has at least a data-transfer rate of 5Gbps for 4K at 60Hz or 10Gbps for 6K. For 8K we recommend you use at least a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 or USB4 cable or 80/120Gbps Thunderbolt 5 cable. The higher the bandwidth, the less risk of signal degradation.
Consider cable length, too. While compression technologies should kick in, the longer your cable, the more the signal can degrade so opt for as short a cable as you require when connecting from your MacBook or dock to a USB-C monitor. A fully featured C-to-C cable that is 1 meter or shorter will work just fine for 95% of what people need. The Cable Matters 10Gbps/100W 1m USB-C Cable is a recommended solution.
If you need a longer cable, a 2m Thunderbolt 4 or 5 cable, such as the Cable Matters 2m Thunderbolt 4 cable. See the reviews above for more options.
Some USB-C monitors can provide between 65W to 90W of passthrough power back to the laptop, so ensure your USB-C cable supports at least 100W if you want to use your USB-C monitor to power your laptop.





2.
Can you convert a Lightning cable to USB-C?
Apple has released a Lightning–to–USB-C adapter—confusingly named the Apple USB-C to Lightning Adapter ($29 at Apple’s U.S. store or £29 at Apple’s UK store) so you can convert an old Lightning cable into a USB-C cable for your new iPhone 15 or later, but, as you might expect from Apple, it’s way more expensive than just buying one of the new and superior USB-C cables we’ve reviewed above.





3.
What is the difference between Active and Passive Thunderbolt cables?
An “active” Thunderbolt cable contains built-in electronic chips that boost and repeat the data signal, allowing it to maintain stable, error-free full-speed (40Gbps) signals over longer distances compared to shorter “passive” cables that lack these chips.

title: How to keep watching DVDs with VLC as Apple phases out Mac DVD support
content:
Apple has started retiring the technology behind its built-in DVD playback starting in macOS 27. Here's how you can still watch discs on a Mac with an optical drive and VLC.

VLC on Mac
For now, the change affects developers, not people watching DVDs on their Macs. Apple has removed the DVDPlayback framework from the macOS 27 SDK, so developers can no longer build apps against it with that SDK.
The framework itself remains in macOS 27, and Apple says it won't be removed until a future release. DVD Player also remains available and functional in macOS 27.
If you have movies on DVD, you don't have to wait for another macOS update to find a different way to play them. The free VLC app can open a DVD as a disc, giving you access to its movie, menus, chapters, audio tracks, and subtitles.

title: 1Password Security Breach: What Was Accessed and What Wasn't
content:
Popular password management app 1Password today said it experienced a security breach earlier this month. 1Password says some customer names and email addresses were accessed, but no customer vault contents were compromised.


On November 19, 1Password saw indications that an employee's GitHub account had been breached and began investigating. The company says the breached GitHub account was used to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, with the code downloading some customer data. Here's a list of what the hacker was able to get:

 	
Names and email addresses customers use to sign into 1Password

 	
Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

 	
Public keys

 	
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (1Password says this can't be used for account access)

 	
Tokens in emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

 	
Other non-secret account data related to 1Password's internal architecture, like version numeric identifiers and file numeric identifiers

 	
1Password source code, which 1Password says does not include customer data or user secrets

 	
Access to 1Password's CI/CD system, which it says has infrastructure-related secrets for the service to work


According to 1Password, there is no impact to its services, availability, or product security. Customer vaults and the items in them were not accessed, nor were the keys that protect vaults. The hacker did not have access to account recovery keys or 1Password apps and browser extensions. 1Password vaults are encrypted and protected by keys on the user end, so content is not accessible to 1Password or anyone who hacks the 1Password servers.

The biggest risk comes from the token breach. Tokens can be used for account recovery, but they only work when paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to a user's email address. Codes have now been changed from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them more difficult to brute force.

The affected GitHub account has been disabled, and the attacker's token was revoked. Internal credentials that may have been exposed have been revoked. Internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls have been "tightened," with new detection methods for similar attacks. The company found no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using the exposed account provisioning tokens, and it has hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its response.

1Password users who had a token accessed were notified, but it is unclear if 1Password has sent notices about the breach to all users. While the blog post is titled as "update on" a security incident, it does not seem that the breach was disclosed when 1Password first learned of it six days ago.

1Password will not contact users to ask for an account password or Secret Key, and the information should be entered only in the official 1Password app or official website. It recommends all users be cautious about phishing attempts like emails, texts, and calls that mention 1Password or account recovery.

title: 1Password has been hacked–passwords are safe, but admin data was accessed
content:
Macworld





1Password is one of the most popular password managers, and one we’ve frequently recommended here at Macworld. Unfortunately, it has just suffered a major security incident.
On November 19, a malicious attacker gained access to a 1Password employee’s corporate GitHub account. They used that to access the 1Password source code and get access to the company’s backend services, which holds the administrative data for customers.
That’s stuff like customer names and email addresses, as well as public keys (but not private keys), account creation and sign-in times, and the like.
The good news for 1Password customers is that the content of user “vaults” were not compromised. That includes passwords and the other info that 1Password stores (like most password managers these days, 1Password can store payment info, addresses, and other data you may wish to auto-fill in forms). 1Password relies on private keys to decrypt passwords and other vault info, which are all hashed and salted so that even if an attacker decrypted one record it couldn’t get access to others.
1Password does not store your account password nor your secret key, which is used to generate the private keys stored on your own devices and necessary to access your encrypted info. All of that stuff is still safe. 
In the wake of the incident, 1Password disabled the GitHub account and revoked its key, rotated or revoked all internal credentials, lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters, and brought in an external cybersecurity firm to audit their efforts.
The company makes the following recommendations to users:
Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
If you see something suspicious, email support@1password.com.
