title: An OLED MacBook Air is coming in 2028. Will it glow?
content:
Macworld





Last year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple has plans to update the MacBook Air with an OLED display in 2028. In his most recent Power On podcast, Gurman reiterated those plans, claiming that OLED will be part of a MacBook Air “overhaul” over the next 12 to 15 months.
The current MacBook Air design was introduced in 2022. While the design is soon-to-be five years old, it doesn’t feel dated and aligns with the other Pros without a touch display. But now that a new laptop design has been introduced with the PROLED XDR Display, Apple will quickly move to update its other laptop designs so they don’t lose momentum.
What would a MacBook Air “overhaul” look like? Even though the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t all that visually different from the mini-LED MacBook Pro that Apple still sells, it’s different enough to set it apart in the line. Besides the OLED display, it features thinner bezels and rounder corners that expand the usable space further toward the bottom of the display (and macOS does a really cool trick with those corners). It also has a Dynamic Island instead of a notch.
More importantly to the Air line, the PROLED laptop is slightly smaller and noticeably lighter. The 14-inch PROLED XDR MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, about a half-pound less than the non-touchscreen model and about a quarter-pound heavier than the 13-inch Air, which weighs 2.7 pounds. If Apple can get the 13-inch Air down to 2.25 pounds or so, it’ll make a dramatic difference.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s major new feature is a touchscreen tandem OLED, but I don’t expect the MacBook Air to get such a high-end screen. These are premium features that Apple will keep on its Pro laptop–a tandem OLED is a costly component to put into an Air. More likely is that the 2028 Air will not have a touchscreen, and it will have a single OLED panel similar to the one in the iPad mini.
So, a thinner, lighter, OLED MacBook Air with more usable screen space. Sounds pretty nice. But what about the glowing Apple logo? It would be cool to see it on the 2028 MacBook Air, but I’m not counting on it. I think Apple will keep it as a MacBook Pro feature to set it apart from the Air and MacBook Neo. But who knows, maybe Apple decided it’s part of the design language covering all its laptops. That would be a nice touch.

title: Apple has made an iPad that runs macOS, but we’ll probably never see it
content:
Macworld





The release of the touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has given new life to an old question in the Apple community: Will Apple ever release macOS on the iPad? We may finally have an answer, and it’s probably not one people are going to like.
On the latest edition of the Power On podcast, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said in no uncertain terms, “At this point, I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon.” Gurman revealed that Apple actually has iPads running macOS within Apple Park, but not for the purpose of releasing macOS on iPad to the general public. It’s for developing Mac-like features for iPadOS such as multitasking, and rebuilding Mac apps like Final Cut Pro for iPad. However, he cautions, “There is no work being done to consumerize macOS on the iPad,” said Gurman.
He’s on the side of the people who aren’t happy with that decision, however. “There are logic for the iPad. So they’re re-building a lot of the Mac and bring it to the iPad piece by piece, versus bringing the whole operating system to the iPad, he said. “In my view, I think they should just launch a 15-, 16-inch iPad and just bring Mac OS to it and just rip the Band-Aid off.”
But Guman notes that there’s another reason for keeping the iPad on iPadOS that’s complicates things further. In the European Union, it’s “better” for Apple to have distinct operating systems for its hardware segments, due to regulations. Considering how Apple swapped out Lightning on the iPhone due to EU regulations, it seems very unlikely that macOS will be released for the iPad.
Gurman does offer one glimmer of hope. Apple has been rumored to be working on a super-sized foldable iPad, something and opens up to a 19- or 20-inch display. Gurman said “it’s been facing a lot of issues” and was originally scheduled for 2027, but it’s been pushed out to 2029, if Apple decided to release it at all. Gurman said Apple is still undecided as to what operating system it will run. It could run macOS, iPadOS, or “something entirely new.”

Annoyingly, most power banks require you to carry around a cable, too. Wireless power banks do away with cables but come with their own major limitation—the inefficiency of wireless charging means you need a high-capacity power bank to fully charge a drained iPhone.
MagSafe is a technology that’s compatible with all iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, Air and Duo models, from the mini to the Pro Max, but strangely missing from the 16e model. It allows accessories to clamp magnetically to the back of the iPhone, making the charging connection more efficient. Most standard magnetic power banks will connect with the iPhone Duo but are too long to maintain a firm grip when handled or placed in a pocket or bag—look for power banks designed specially for that model..

You should consider size when it comes to a power bank: physical size and battery capacity. The higher the battery capacity, the more recharging power you’ll get from the power bank—but you’ll also be carrying around a larger, heavier item. Lighter, slimmer power banks are easier to pocket even when clamped to your phone. Larger power banks might not fit in your trouser pocket and can slide off easier when pocketed even if clamped magnetically.
10K power banks (with a 10000mAh battery capacity) can charge a phone close to two times over, while 5K (5000mAh) battery packs usually stretch between 60-75%, which is often enough to get you to the next wall-socket powering opportunity. If you are relying on the power bank for long-haul travel or a camping trip, a 10K battery or higher will suit you better. Belkin even offers a mid-range 8K power bank.
Milliamp hours (mAh) is quite a blunt measurement of battery capacity. It’s great for quickly differentiating between power bank sizes but we also list the capacity in the more accurate watt hours (Wh).
Also, look out for power banks that are built using the latest semi-solid-state battery technology that uses less liquid electrolyte than standard litium-ion power banks, making them more durable, longer lasting, and safer.
Wireless power bank charging speed
Wireless charging speeds vary from 7.5W (MagSafe Compatible) to 15W (certified MagSafe and Qi2), all the way to the very fastest wireless charging at 25W (Qi2.2). While it’s not as efficient as using a cable to charge a phone, magnetic wireless charging is a step closer to doing away with cables altogether. Qi2 25W brings wireless charging close to wired speed but only iPhones 16 and later support that speed, and some power banks include a built-in USB-C cable for even faster charging up to 45W. The iPhone Air can manage 20W max on even a 25W charger. See Which wireless tech is best for your iPhone?.
We have listed the speeds at which each portable power bank can be charged itself (Input charger) and charge the iPhone (Output charger). The higher the wattage, the faster the charging should be.

How we tested
MagSafe charger testing was conducted using an iPhone 16, 17 or 18 Pro, subscribed to a 5G network and WiFi, with screen off and all default settings.
Our test is a simple battery recharge shootout. We let our test-unit iPhone Pro (3095mAh battery capacity) drain to just 10% and then set the Battery Pack to work recharging the phone. We then assigned the charger a score of whatever percentage it managed to charge the iPhone to and subtract the 10%; we test each model at least twice.
It’s not a real-world test of day-to-day use where you’ll likely be using your phone for various tasks (of varying battery usage) and in different environmental conditions and network configurations. But it does give us a common score format that we can use to compare different battery-pack models.

				
					

				
			
Why is magnetic wireless better?
The MagSafe connection to Apple’s iPhone is precise enough to make wireless charging more efficient as around 20% of non-magnetic power loss is from poor placement of a phone and the wireless charging pad. Standard Qi wireless charging can lose as much as 50% of the portable battery’s power, but MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging loses ‘just’ 30%. Hot out of the gadget laboratory, the new Qi 2.2 (also known as Qi2 25W) brings even faster 25W wireless charging for the iPhone 16, 17 and 18. 15% will be plenty fast enough for most of us but who doesn’t want the fastest possible charging when your iPhone’s battery icon is in the red?
Why comparing Watt Hours is better than Milliamp Hours
Phone batteries are generally rated in Milliamp Hours (mAh) but this is a measure of electrical charge, while a Watt Hour is equal to one watt of energy consumed for one hour of time.
When comparing battery capacities and how much a power pack will boost a phone’s internal battery, energy is more important than electrical charge.
And mAh ignores a battery voltage, which determines the wattage (power) of a battery.
If the mAh is the same, the higher the voltage, the greater the actual stored power.
For example, Apple’s MagSafe Battery Pack is rated at just 1460mAh but it has a higher voltage potential (7.62V) than the iPhone (3.81V) or other battery packs, meaning that it can provide more power to an iPhone than its mAh suggests; in fact, it is actually 2920mAh.
To go into further depth about this read our feature iPhone battery capacities compared that also lists all iPhones battery life in mAh and Wh.
Anatomy of a magnetic power bank

				
					

				
			
TORRAS




A lot more than a battery goes into the making of a magnetic power bank.
Of course, the battery is the most important component, but the wireless charging coils and magnetic connection are vital for efficient and therefore fast and powerful charging. The transmitter coil transfers power by electromagnetic induction.
The magnets need to be set up to exactly connect the transmitting coils—here on the power bank— to the receiving coils, in this case inside the iPhone.
The example shown above is the Torras MagStall Wireless Power Bank, reviewed in our chart. You can see the various parts, including that power bank’s rotating stand/handle.
Which magnetic wireless tech is right for each iPhone?
iPhone 7 and earlier: Don’t support wireless charging. 
iPhone 8 – iPhone X/XS/XR: Support wireless charging. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly at 7.5W but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 11 and earlier: Don’t support MagSafe. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 12 – iPhone 15: Support MagSafe and Qi2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, and at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers.
iPhone 16 – iPhone 18, plus iPhone Duo: Support MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2.2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers, and at 25W with Qi2.2-certified power banks and chargers.
Is charging via a cable faster or safer than magnetic wireless charging?
Charging via a cable is nearly always faster than wireless, even the latest Qi2.2 wireless chargers. Wireless charging is inefficient, losing some of its energy transfer through heat, for example. MagSafe, Qi2, and Qi2.2 magnetic connections dramatically improve efficiency but sticking a cable in is still a faster method, if not as convenient.
Most magnetic wireless power banks include at least one USB-C port, and some even include a port and an integrated cable for ultimate convenience. Models after the iPhone 17 can charge to 50% in 20 minutes or under via a cable and a 45W or higher charger or power bank. But wireless is so simple and cable-free that we don’t mind waiting an extra 15 minutes or so to reach such a charge wirelessly.
Why does my phone occasionally charge slowly or even stop charging?
This phone charging behavior is due to the built-in battery management feature on your iPhone. A phone heats up during charging as power is exchanged between the charger’s coils and the iPhone’s own. The phone actively adjust its charging behavior accordingly. This can slow down or temporarily pause charging to protect battery health and extend its lifespan. This is completely normal. Once the phone cools down, charging will automatically resume as normal.
What is a semi solid state battery?
The material that carries ions back and forth inside a battery is called “electrolyte”. Traditional lithium-ion batteries use a volatile, free-flowing liquid for electrolyte. As their name suggests, solid-state batteries use a solid material such as a ceramic or polymer. But semi-solid-state batteries are more common in today’s new generation of power banks.
A semi-solid-state battery uses a mix of solid particles in a much smaller amount of liquid, making a hybrid thick gel, paste or slurry. By reducing the liquid content to a minimum, semi-solid-state batteries increase stability and durability and significantly lower the risk of leaks, fires, and dangerous thermal runaway.
What about non-wireless power banks?
Wireless charging—especially magnetic wireless charging—is super convenient and does away with the need to carry around messy cables to connect your device to the battery pack.
But wired charging is nearly always faster and not much of an inconvenience if you are not out and about. Over on our sister site Tech Advisor I have reviewed the best power banks that includes standard non-wireless battery packs that might be a decent solution as well as the power banks reviewed above.
Do magnetic power banks work when the iPhone is in a case?
Yes, most quality iPhone cases are compatible with MagSafe having their own magnet ring to ensure a close connection between the power bank’s magnetic charging coils and the iPhone’s own. You can find exactly which are supported in our roundups of the best iPhone 18 cases, best iPhone 17 cases, and best iPhone 16 cases.

title: Apple Has an iPhone Notifications Problem
content:
Apple has rules in place that are supposed to protect iPhone users from unwanted advertising in push notifications and Live Activities, but some apps appear to be flouting these rules, and Apple does not appear to be consistently enforcing them.


Apple's App Store guidelines do allow iPhone apps to send push notifications for promotions or direct marketing purposes, but only if users have "explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed" in the app, and so long as the app provides a method "for a user to opt out from receiving such messages."

Push Notifications should not be used for promotions or direct marketing purposes unless customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app's UI, and you provide a method in your app for a user to opt out from receiving such messages.
Unfortunately, there are some examples of apps ignoring this guideline.

On my iPhone in Canada, there are several apps that send me push notifications containing promotions without offering a way to opt out of these promotion-specific notifications, such as Cineplex, McDonald's, and Wendy's.

Canadian food delivery app Skip does offer a setting to turn off promotional notifications, but it has continued to send them to me long after I opted out.


Do you have any iOS apps that don't respect your promo notification settings or don't let you turn off promo notifications as Apple requires?

Let me know for a MacRumors story!

— Joe Rossignol (@rsgnl) November 25, 2026



A few MacRumors readers informed us that after they turned off DoorDash notifications for offers specifically and then place a delivery order, the app will prompt users to re-enable notifications so they "never miss an order update," even though they still have notifications enabled for order updates. The wording of this prompt can trick users into thinking that they might not receive order updates, but tapping the button re-enables offers.

app design guidelines saying "don't use a Live Activity to display ads or promotions" under "best practices." Apple's App Store guidelines say apps should not send users "unsolicited messages" via Live Activities.


Never expected to see anything like this https://t.co/GbdRIfqaE2
— Out of Galaxy (@OutofGalaxyy) November 22, 2026



If you know of other offending apps, let us know in the comments section. There are more.

Apple recently sent out its own App Store notification advertising a Paramount+ subscription deal, but the App Store does offer an option to opt out. Open the App Store, tap on your profile picture in the top-right corner, tap on Notifications, and turn off Recommendations & Offers. However, it is not clear if Apple obtained explicit consent from users as its App Store guidelines require. Of course, the App Store is a preinstalled app, so it technically does not have to follow the rules that Apple sets for third-party App Store apps.


PUSH ads now?! https://t.co/WRBndvxbE3
— Dylan (@DylanMcD8) November 21, 2026



All in all, it appears that Apple needs to do more to crack down on apps that are violating its rules surrounding advertising in push notifications and Live Activities.

title: Apple Is Far From Done With 2026: Here's What's Still Coming
content:
Apple's busiest season isn't over yet – far from it. With Black Friday kicking off this week, plus new products, software updates, and new smart home accessories running into December, there's more on the way from Apple before the end of 2026, so be sure to stick around.


Below, we've rounded up what's still coming, along with one date in particular that's worth watching if you're a holiday shopper.


Black Friday – November 27: Not a product launch unfortunately, but a date likely worth marking. Apple's annual four-day shopping event runs from Friday, November 27 through Monday, November 30, with gift cards worth up to $300 offered with eligible purchases. Apple is also offering new and qualified returning subscribers the Apple TV streaming service for $6.99 per month for six months, with that deal available until November 30. Our Black Friday roundup will be tracking all the deals.

(PRODUCT)RED AirPods Max 2 and HomePod mini 2 – expected December 1: Apple plans to release (PRODUCT)RED versions of the existing AirPods Max 2 and HomePod mini 2 on or around Tuesday, December 1, which is World AIDS Day, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The new color is expected to be the only change. Apple is also releasing a red Wrist Strap for AirPods Pro and a red Sport Band for the Apple Watch.

App Store Awards – expected December: Apple named this year's finalists on November 18, and the winners are expected in the coming weeks. Last year, Apple announced the winners on December 4, so a similar early-December date looks likely this year.

Apple Music Replay – expected December: The full 2026 Replay recap is likely to arrive around the same time as last year's, when the full version became available on December 2, with your top songs, artists, and listening stats for the year.

iOS 27.3 – December: Apple says iOS 27.3 will be released to the public in December, though it hasn't given a date. The first iOS 27.3 beta arrived on Tuesday, November 3. Beta features can change before release, but so far it includes new Siri AI actions across apps, vertical tabs and an Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, the redesigned Health app, a new Apple Fitness+ Gym Strength workout that builds a four-week plan, and more. Our iOS 27.3 beta guide has the full list.

Apple Intelligence in China – December: The first Apple Intelligence features for users in China are already in testing in the iOS 27.3 beta, and Apple has confirmed the public rollout for December alongside the update. Apple has partnered with Alibaba to add Qwen support to Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence. The initial release is for supported iPhones, with other platforms to follow after the required regulatory approvals, and it does not include Siri AI.

Apple Home Collection – from December: The new Apple-backed, third-party lineup includes smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple says that availability begins in December, although select accessories will not arrive until early 2027.

title: macOS Tahoe’s enormous window corner radii make so much sense now
content:
Macworld





Back when macOS 26 Tahoe was introduced, the corner radius was something of a controversy. For reasons unbeknownst to users, Apple opted to increase the roundness of the window corners, from 10-point on previous versions of macOS to 26-point in Tahoe.
The slight change was extremely noticeable. Windows looked amateurish, older apps didn’t match the new style, and even Apple was inconsistent within its own default apps. And what’s worse, windows were harder to resize when trying to grab them by the corner—it was a mess. To make matters worse, the windows didn’t even match the corners of the Mac’s screen. The 26-point radius was closer to the iPhone than a MacBook or iMac, and everyone just assumed the change was due to laziness or poor quality control.
In macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple changed back to a more sensible 20-point radius. People rejoiced and assumed Apple listened to the criticism, realized its mistake, and made the necessary adjustments.
But now I’m not so sure it was a mistake. I hadn’t realized this before, but the new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii. And you can actually see it in action. Check out this gif:

				
					

				
			
Roman Loyola/Foundry




What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.
So it seems like what we thought was a bit of lazy design was just a peek at what was to come from the MacBook. Back then there wasn’t a curve at the bottom of MacBook screens, so there was nothing to see yet, and the overly rounded corners were something of an experimentation for a machine that was still in development.
So remember, Apple may make mistakes, but it doesn’t usually do things by accident—even if we might not like the explanation.

title: Anthropic unveils Claude-powered easy button for making Mac apps
content:
Macworld





Anthropic announced Tuesday that it is rolling out beta access to a new feature in Claude for Macs that allows users to save “artifacts” as apps. When a user creates an artifact app, it appears like a native Mac app that opens in its own window, rather than in the Claude app, essentially operating as an independent app. Artifact apps have their own icons and can be shared with others like normal Mac apps.
Artifacts are projects that users create in Claude separately from the standard chat interface. Users can describe what they want their project to do, and Claude will create it. Users can adjust, edit, and tweak the design and functionality either manually or through conversations with Claude. They typically live inside a separate section in its sidebar for artifacts, and users typically use this space for creating things such as documents, graphics, code, and other projects. Artifacts are available on all Anthropic plans: Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans.
Artifact apps can use Claude and its connectors, and they automatically update whenever someone with permissions makes changes. Apps can send notifications or add items to the Mac menu bar or system tray. However, any requests the artifact app makes count towards your plan’s usage limits. Anthropic shared a list of apps created by people at the company:
Vitals, a menu bar and tray app for peeking at your computer’s performance
Linnet, a full layered image editor
Phosphor, a file manager that looks made for a movie set
Sift, which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized
Tern, a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain
The artifact app creation beta is rolling out on all Claude plans but is not available to HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments. The Claude app is required to launch an artifact app.

title: Claude Now Lets You Install Artifacts as Desktop Apps
content:
Anthropic has released a new feature for Claude that allows users to install artifacts as desktop apps on macOS and Windows.


Artifacts are documents, designs, dashboards, and interactive tools that Claude creates in a panel alongside your chat, where you can view and edit them.

When you ask Claude to create an artifact, you can now click "Install as app" in the Share menu, after which you'll be able to launch it in its own dedicated app window and see it in the Dock.

Artifact-based apps don't need to be packaged or signed, but they do need a permission level to be set. Choosing Default permissions means they can only do what they'd be able to do in a browser, while giving them higher App permissions means they can do things like create always-on-top windows, listen for global keyboard shortcuts, and send notifications. Full computer access means apps can run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time.

made some example apps available to try and to give users an idea of what's possible.



Anthropic says building an app and any calls it makes to Claude count toward usage limits. The feature remains in beta and is available on all plans in Claude Desktop, though Enterprise users will need to switch it on manually first.

title: Black Friday iPhone Duo deals: Your best chance to get one
content:
Macworld





The iPhone Duo is definitely making waves as Apple’s first foldable phone. Some users just have to have one and are looking at Black Friday sales in hopes of finding a discount. It is, after all, Apple’s most expensive iPhone ever.
Because the iPhone Duo is in such short supply, it can be difficult to find one in stock at all and even harder to find any sort of discount. Here are the best places to look.
Direct from Apple
Apple’s physical stores get in a small amount of stock regularly, but it’s impossible to predict it ahead of time, and they’re gone in a flash. See “stock tracking services” below to try to get an upper hand on it.
You can buy an iPhone Duo from Apple online, and the delivery estimate has gotten a lot better in recent days. Apple’s online store used to say to expect delivery in late January; now it’s saying 4-5 weeks or December 23 to January 5 for most orders. Some users report getting their order earlier than estimated. So there’s a chance you’ll still get your iPhone Duo before Christmas, if that’s your concern.
Big-box stores
Stores like Best Buy and Walmart seem to have limited stock, but there are some caveats. Only certain configurations are listed as ready to ship, typically those with more storage (and a higher price). They also require activating a new line on a carrier for which the store has a deal, typically T-Mobile, AT&T, or Verizon. Then you can pay the full price up front, or pay in monthly installments for several years. 
These are very nearly the same deals as buying direct from carrier stores, which you’ll find below. With limited stock available, it may be your preferred option.
Carrier deals
Carriers offer the “deals” on new iPhones every year, and they all take the same general setup: You have to activate a line on the carrier, and you have to buy the phone in monthly installments for usually 24 to 36 months. Your big discount comes in the form of bill credits toward those monthly installments. It’s common for carriers to limit these deals only to those who are on more premium phone plans, and some require you to trade in an eligible device.
In other words, it’s a way to lock you in to an expensive carrier plan for two or three years. If you leave the carrier or switch to a cheaper, unsupported plan, you’re on the hook for the remainder of the full phone price.
AT&T: No configurations shipping until January when we checked the website. The deal is $1,200 off as monthly bill credits for 36 months, with a qualifying trade-in.
Verizon: Verizon is currently showing delivery times in mid-December. The company offers “free” Apple Watch SE 3 & AirPods 5, as bill credits over 36 months, and you need a service plan for that Apple Watch.
T-Mobile: Current orders show that they’re shipping in January, and you get up to $2,100 of your purchase back as monthly bill credits. Only certain plans qualify.
In addition to the “big three” U.S. carriers, many of the MVNOs that use their networks (such as Xfinity, Mint Mobile, Boost Mobile, and others) offer the iPhone Duo for purchase, and some even have financing deals like the major carriers. They appear to be largely out of stock as well, with ship times estimated in mid-December through January.
Stock-tracking services
Whenever there is anything in short supply, you’ll find websites and services that will look for it to become in stock and notify you so you can jump on the purchase right away. Event tickets, sneakers, game consoles, you name it.
There are quite a lot of stock-checking sites that promise to be the very best choice for locating an iPhone Duo. (Believe me, we’ve gotten emails from all of them asking to be listed in our articles.) Here’s a sampling of them. We don’t have any way of knowing which is actually “the best,” and their inclusion here is not an official endorsement. This is just a sampling to get you started if you want to use such a service.
iPhoneStockChecker shows you nearby stock in various colors and storage sizes. 
OrionChime has two sub-sites. The one we are interested in checks stock for Apple products like iPhones, Mac Studio, or Mac mini.
Apple Inventory Check also checks inventory for various Apple products, including Macs and Apple Watch, and of course iPhones (including Duo). It’s limited to Apple Stores, but it’s faster than using the interface on Apple’s site to check availability of various configurations.
TrackaLacker is a general stock-tracking site for online retailers. You can watch iPhone Duo there, but only for the online stores of places like Best Buy or Walmart, not the Apple Store online or in-store stock.
InStock Tracker tracks all sorts of products, including iPhones.
Best Black Friday iPhone deals
Buying an iPhone from the U.K.? If it doesn’t have to be an iPhone Duo you can save hundreds on a new iPhone at Amazon right now. Here are our picks of the best Black Friday iPhone deals.

Many purchase portable monitors not for their portability but instead their versatility and ease of use—so it can be moved across a home or corporate office. At home, it could let you have two home office setups without having to purchase two monitors, or simply store the monitor out of sight in a cupboard when not in use. In an office, it could be carried to meetings if you need to lead a presentation or study a large spreadsheet. I’ve been on many a call, trying to keep on track on my MacBook as the presenter talks through a complex Excel doc. As large a portable monitor as possible is what you need in those situations—or a wide TV screen.

title: Tidal Bans AI Music, While Apple Music Sticks to Labels
content:
Streaming music service Tidal today said it plans to start blocking AI music on December 9. Any track generated entirely with AI will be removed from the platform, with Tidal rejecting AI songs in the future.


Tidal lead Robert Andersen said 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days have been flagged as AI-generated. Approximately 29 million songs will be deleted and Tidal expects 80,000 to 85,000 songs to be rejected per day.

AI music will start disappearing on December 9 and will be "completely gone" at the beginning of 2027. AI-assisted music will continue to be allowed, since the policy is only for songs made entirely with AI tools. Tidal previously demonetized AI music, but removing it goes a step further.

Andersen said Tidal believes the move will "resonate with both artists and listeners alike" because 96 percent of AI songs get zero plays.

Apple Music, but it introduced AI Transparency Tags earlier this year. Apple is relying on labels and distributors to disclose when AI has been used, and it said in August that tracks "materially generated using AI" must have a "Made With AI" label.

title: Add Holiday Lights and Snow to Your Mac With Festivitas
content:
Festivitas is a fun little holiday-themed Mac app that developer Simon Støvring introduced two years ago and has been updating since. Its main purpose is to add lights to the Mac's Dock and menu bar, but there's also a version for the iPhone and iPad.


The holiday 2026 Festivitas update adds new customizations. For the first time, you can upload custom bulb shapes. There's an option to import an image and convert it to a bulb in a string of lights. Simple PNGs on a transparent background produce the best results, and for more complex images, bulbs can use the original colors.

You can customize light shapes, color, size, opacity, drop height, cable thickness, and more in the Settings. Lights can animate with different patterns, like pulse, twinkle, chase, and wave.

There are pointer decorations like sparkles, bubbles, falling leaves, confetti, a Christmas tree, a wreath, and more. Falling snow will now pile up on top of app windows for an added holiday effect. You can adjust snow rate, density, and flake size.

Snow and lights can be displayed above app windows or just on the desktop, with lights also visible on the Dock. Shortcuts can be used to play music and turn on lights, activate the snow effect if the weather forecast includes snow, and start a snowstorm.

Along with custom bulb shapes and falling snow, Festivitas for the iPhone and ‌iPad‌ now fully transparent animated widgets on the without a screenshot workaround.

Festivitas for Mac requires some accessibility access to work. I asked Støvring about Apple's planned permission changes in macOS 27.3, and how they will affect the Festivitas app. He said Festivitas gets far more access than it needs because Apple's options aren't granular enough, and he'd prefer to ask for less access.

Menu bar lights, snow, and pointer effects work without the System & App Protection Override permission, while lights in the Dock and snow landing on windows require access.

downloaded from the Festivitas website. The iPhone and ‌iPad‌ app is available for free from the App Store, and it too offers customer-selected fair pricing between $3.99 and $9.99. The updates are free for existing users. [Direct Link]

title: Google Says Apple's iOS Browser Rules Offer 'Choice on Paper, Not in Practice'
content:
Google's Chrome for Developers team today supported Mozilla's complaint about Apple's rules on non-WebKit browser engines in the European Union, calling out restrictions that make launching an alternative engine too difficult.


Mozilla recently joined a coalition of up to 55,000 businesses and organizations to ask the European Commission to force Apple to change its browser rules. Apple started allowing alternative browser engines in the EU in early 2024, but the coalition says no browser maker has been able to transfer its EU users from Apple's WebKit engine to a new engine because of Apple's conditions.

Mozilla explained that using its Gecko browser engine instead of WebKit would require releasing a second Firefox app. Apple says apps with alternative browser engines have to be distributed only in the EU, so Mozilla has been unable to add Gecko to its existing app. Firefox users in the EU would need to transfer to a new app and move all their content, and many users might not be willing to switch. Mozilla said Apple's conditions are "unworkable" and that Apple has only complied with the EU's Digital Markets Act "on paper."

Chrome for Developers echoed the statement in its X post:
We agree with @mozilla. Nearly 3 years after alternative browser engines on iOS were EU-mandated, zero launched due to remaining Apple restrictions. Forcing browsers to ship separate apps and re-acquire users is choice on paper, not in practice.

Though one Google team expressed support for Mozilla, Google did not sign the open letter to the European Commission. In 2023, Google started work on an experimental version of Chromium for iOS with the Blink engine, but Google said it was only a prototype that would not be released.

participated in a DMA workshop where Mozilla brought up iOS support for third-party browser engines. According to Mozilla, Apple claimed Google and Mozilla have "everything they need" to ship an alternative browser engine in the EU and "have chosen not to do so." In its documentation for alternative browser engines, Apple says its requirements help keep users safe online.

is in talks with Apple over its browser engine restrictions. It is also consulting Mozilla and other signatories on how rival browsers can compete with Safari on Apple devices.

title: These gifts every Apple fan will love all cost less than AirPods 5
content:
Macworld






The holiday season is upon us, and picking the right gifts for our favorite people can be challenging. We want to skip the cliché socks this year, but spending a grand on a new iPhone or iPad isn’t in the cards, either. Luckily, Apple and other reputable brands sell a wide range of helpful gadgets that top out at $129. Even without breaking the bank, these practical picks are guaranteed to impress anyone on your list for months to come.



AirPods 5

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




The AirPods 5 are the benchmark for this list, so we had to include them. Despite maintaining the same $129 starting price as their predecessors, the entry-level AirPods 5 now come with ANC for the first time, essentially a $50 price cut over the AirPods 4. Beyond muffling external noise, the ANC technology unlocks Apple’s Live Translation feature, which lets users chat more naturally with locals when traveling internationally.
Other neat perks include support for immersive Spatial Audio content, water and dust resistance, Automatic Device Switching, and Siri AI commands. It’s a well-rounded pair of wireless earbuds that will seamlessly connect to all of their Apple devices, providing a comfortable listening experience.
Shopping tip: You can save some money if you shop for AirPods at Amazon and other retailers. It often sells the AirPods below the MSRP. AirPods 5 haven’t yet gone on sale, but be sure to check for any Black Friday deals.






MagSafe wallet

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani/Foundry




Ever since Apple baked MagSafe into the iPhone, magnetic wallets have boomed in popularity, especially among minimalists aiming to carry fewer separate items. The Apple FineWoven Wallet with MagSafe ($59 MSRP; $53 on Amazon) is one of the most stylish options, offering a slender design, several colors, native Find My support with detachment alerts, and room for up to three cards. While the FineWoven material doesn’t age as gracefully as its leather forefather, it does get the job done for a few years.
If you’re looking for something cheaper, larger, more versatile, or just generally different, you can check out the various MagSafe wallets listed on Amazon and pick a positively rated product. Before proceeding, ensure the recipient has a compatible iPhone model, as the Duo does not support standard-size wallets (including Apple’s official accessory), and some lower-end variants like the 16e miss out on MagSafe altogether.






AirTag with Key Ring

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani/Foundry




The AirTag 2 ($29.99 MSRP; $23 on Amazon) is one of the safest and most inexpensive gifts on this list, as iPhone users can never have enough of these reliable Bluetooth trackers. They could toss one in their backpack, purse, or luggage to pinpoint its exact location using the Find My app at all times. And with the second-gen model upgrading the speaker and detection range, the coin-sized tracker is louder and easier to find than ever before.
If you’re looking to spend a bit more on this gift, you could pair it with Apple’s AirTag FineWoven Key Ring ($35 MSRP; available on Amazon), helping the recipient attach it to keys and other items more easily.






Apple Pencil (USB-C)

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry





This one is for the valued creatives in your life. Whether they have an iPad with a USB-C port or an iPhone Duo, the USB-C Apple Pencil ($79 MSRP; $49 on Amazon) will supercharge their doodling and note-taking experience. The official stylus supports precise input and tilt sensitivity, making it more dependable for illustration and writing down everyday thoughts than using one’s finger.






Google Fitbit Air

				
					

				
			
Thomas Deehan / Foundry





While Apple Watches are deemed the best overall fitness trackers for casual iPhone users, the cheapest SE model starts at a whopping $249. Fortunately, the third-party alternatives are plentiful, and many of them cost way less. Google’s Fitbit Air ($99 MSRP; available on Amazon) is a screen-less activity tracker with a one-week battery life, offering personalized insights, heart rate measurements, workout recording, sleep tracking, and much more for a lot less money. Any iPhone user can set it up using the Google Health app on iOS and collect metrics similar to those provided by an Apple Watch. It’s the perfect gift for those planning to be more active in 2027.






Nanoleaf smart light strip

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani/Foundry





Christmas is right around the corner, and the Nanoleaf Essentials Matter Lightstrip ($70 MSRP; $45 on Amazon) is the ideal gift for that one friend who hasn’t yet finished setting up their decorations. The smart home product ties directly into Apple HomeKit, enabling native automations, remote control, Control Center access, and much more. It features hundreds of LEDs with separate color zones, letting users opt for a vibrant festive look. After the holidays, they can pair it to their desktop computer or TV to match on-screen hues and create an atmospheric experience or sync to playing music. We’ve linked to the model with 300 LEDs, but Nanoleaf has a variety of lights available.






Sony DualSense controller

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani/Foundry





Now that newer iPhones, iPads, Macs, and even Apple TVs pack ultrafast processors capable of running demanding software, game controllers have become widely sought-after gifts. Sony’s DualSense controller ($75 MSRP; $54 on Amazon) is arguably the best choice for Apple users, as it is natively supported by the operating systems. This unlocks advanced features, such as color customization, button remapping, profile creation, and more. And with support for multiple simultaneous connections, your friend could bring their controller over when visiting you to play local multiplayer games on a single Apple device.






Belkin 3-in-1 wireless charger

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary





Belkin’s $100 Wireless 3-in-1 Foldable Fast Charging Station ($100 MSRP; $77 on Amazon) is suitable for a friend who’s heavily invested in the Apple ecosystem. The charger can accommodate an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods case at the same time, which can help minimize cables and declutter their desk. Thanks to its flexible design, they could use it in pad or stand mode as needed.






Anker power bank

				
					

				
			
Dominik Tomaszewski / Foundry





For portable power, Anker’s Zolo Power Bank ($30 MSRP; $24.69 on Amazon) offers a 10,000mAh battery capacity and 30W fast charging support. It connects to iPhones, iPads, and MacBooks via USB-C, providing uninterrupted charging on the go for all of their Apple devices.






Apple Gift Card

				
					

				
			
Apple





If you’re unsure what exactly your friend needs, you can’t go wrong with an Apple Gift Card. You can set the value to as little as $15 or increase it depending on your budget. You can even customize its design, include a heartfelt message, and schedule it in advance. Amazon will then deliver it via text, email, or a physical package depending on your choice. Once redeemed, your friend will be able to spend the amount on apps, compatible digital purchases, and subscription services or it can be used toward a pricier purchase from the Apple Store.

title: Signal Now Blocks AI Screen Access to Protect Chats
content:
Signal is extending screenshot-blocking protections to iPhones and supported Android devices to prevent AI assistants such as Siri and Gemini from capturing private conversations.


In its announcement, Signal said AI assistants can capture messages displayed on screen, potentially exposing conversations to processing outside the app. End-to-end encryption protects message delivery, but cannot prevent another app from reading messages visible on a recipient's device.

iOS 27, the new "Block ‌Siri‌ AI" setting is enabled by default in Signal version 8.37 or later. It blocks screenshots, screen recordings, and AI screen-reading. On supported Android devices running Signal 8.35.1 or later, screen security activates when an AI assistant attempts to read the screen.

Settings → Privacy → Block Siri AI, either permanently or for 10 minutes to take a screenshot. Apple also offers an Excluded Apps setting under Settings → Siri that prevents ‌Siri‌ from accessing selected apps.

Is free antivirus for Mac good enough?
Free antivirus software can provide basic protection, but it often lacks advanced features such as ransomware protection, firewalls and real-time web security. Paid options offer more comprehensive, all-round protection.
Apple includes built-in security tools like XProtect and Gatekeeper, which block known malware and unverified apps. However, in our testing, it was still possible to install Mac malware or suspicious software if warnings were ignored, showing that Apple’s protections alone are not foolproof.
Free third-party antivirus tools offer an advantage in that they are updated more frequently and can protect against a wider range of threats, including adware, spyware, trojans and ransomware.
The core antivirus engine is often the same in both free and paid versions. The difference lies in the extra features included in premium suites, such as web and phishing protection, VPNs, identity monitoring, parental controls and customer support.
Ultimately, you get what you pay for. If security is a priority, a paid antivirus offers the most complete protection. However, if you’re on a tight budget, a free antivirus is still better than relying solely on Apple’s built-in security tools.

Why you can trust Macworld for antivirus advice
Macworld has been testing Mac software since the launch of the Mac in 1984, giving us decades of experience and deep expertise in Apple’s ecosystem. We understand how Macs work – and how best to protect them.

Our recommendations are based on a combination of independent lab data, structured testing and real-world usage – not just specifications or vendor claims. We regularly review and update our rankings to reflect the latest threats, software updates and performance improvements.
How we test Mac antivirus software
To identify the best antivirus software for Mac, we combine hands-on testing, real-world threat simulation and independent lab data. Our goal is to assess how effectively each product protects your Mac without compromising performance, usability or value.
Real-world testing environment: We begin with a clean installation of macOS, which is then cloned for each antivirus product. Each app is installed and tested in isolation to ensure results are not affected by other software — particularly important as antivirus tools can sometimes flag each other as threats.

Downloading known malware samples
Visiting malicious and phishing websites
Testing suspicious files and drive-by downloads
Running malware in controlled conditions
This allows us to evaluate how well each product detects and blocks both online and offline threats, including Mac-specific malware, adware and potentially unwanted programs (PUPs). We also assess how effectively each tool detects and handles Windows-based malware, which can still pose a risk when sharing files.

 Best Mac Antivirus: FAQ 


1.
Do Macs need antivirus software?
Yes – while Macs are generally more secure than Windows PCs and include built-in protections like XProtect and sandboxing, which helps limit how far malware can spread, these measures are not enough to defend against modern threats such as phishing, adware and ransomware. 
Adding a dedicated antivirus tool helps close those gaps, provides broader coverage against evolving threats and extra layer of security when browsing the web or downloading files.
For more detail, see our guide to whether Macs need antivirus, along with our Mac security tips and advice on how to remove a virus from a Mac.
Do iPhones need antivirus software? 
You may be considering a Mac Antivirus that also offers to protect your iPhone, but is that protection really necessary? 
Apple’s iOS is designed with strong built-in security, including app sandboxing, strict App Store review processes and system-level protections that prevent traditional viruses from infecting your device. This makes it very difficult for malware to spread in the same way it can on other platforms. So, no – iPhones generally don’t need antivirus software.
However, iPhones are not completely risk-free. Threats like phishing attacks, malicious websites and data breaches can still affect users. Instead of installing an antivirus app the best advice is to keep iOS up to date, avoid clicking on suspicious links, use strong passwords and two-factor authentication, and don’t download anything unless you are sure it is safe. 





2.
How does antivirus software protect your Mac?
Mac antivirus software protects your device using a combination of on-demand scans and real-time (always-on) protection.
On-demand scanning checks files when you run a manual or scheduled scan. This can take time, especially on systems with lots of data, and may temporarily use more system resources. For best results, scans are often scheduled to run at convenient times. See how to scan a Mac for malware
Real-time protection works continuously in the background. If malware arrives – for example via an email attachment or downloaded file – the antivirus can detect and block it immediately. Suspicious files are typically quarantined, meaning they are moved to a secure location where they can’t cause harm while you decide whether to delete or restore them.
The effectiveness of these two layers of protection is the most important factor when choosing antivirus software, but additional features can also make a difference.
Many Mac antivirus tools now include ransomware protection, which prevents unauthorised apps from accessing sensitive folders such as Documents or Photos. Only trusted apps are allowed access, and you can customise these permissions.
Web protection is another key feature, often delivered via browser extensions. This helps block malicious websites, phishing attempts and unsafe downloads, reducing the risk of accidentally exposing personal information.





3.
Should my Mac antivirus include a VPN?
Yes, a VPN can be a useful addition to Mac antivirus software. It encrypts your internet connection, helping protect your data – especially on public Wi-Fi. However, built-in VPNs are often limited, so a dedicated VPN service usually offers better performance and features.
Some Mac antivirus packages include a built-in VPN (virtual private network), although VPNs are also widely available as standalone products. For many users, VPNs are appealing because they can mask your location and allow access to region-restricted content, such as streaming services.
More importantly, a VPN improves security by encrypting your internet connection, which is particularly useful when using public Wi-Fi networks. This helps protect your data from interception and reduces the risk of cyberattacks.
While we generally recommend a dedicated Mac VPN service for the best performance and features, a VPN included with antivirus software can still be a useful extra. Just be aware that bundled VPNs often come with limitations, such as data caps or reduced functionality, and may prompt you to upgrade to a full subscription.





4.
What is the best value Mac antivirus?
Value means different things to different users. For some, it’s the best free option; for others, it’s a reasonably priced product with the most useful features. We define value as the best overall balance of protection, performance and features – and for protecting a single Mac, we believe Intego offers the best value.
That said, there are ways to save money on even the top antivirus products. Most Mac antivirus apps are sold as annual subscriptions, often with significant discounts for the first year. When that period ends, you can switch providers to take advantage of new introductory offers, or opt for longer-term plans (such as two- or three-year subscriptions) to reduce the overall cost.
Many antivirus suites also cover multiple devices, including Windows PCs and Android smartphones. If you have several devices in your household, a multi-device plan can offer excellent value. 
For the latest offers, see our guide to the Best Mac Antivirus deals, which includes the most affordable options.





5.
How to spot fake Mac antivirus software?
Because many of us are waking up to the idea that malware is a threat to the Mac, malware writers have made it their business to play on that fear. There have been cases of malware writers disguising their viruses as antivirus apps – two notable examples are Mac Auto Fixer and MacDefender. It’s important to always read reviews on reputable sites such as Macworld before installing any software on your Mac or MacBook.
At the same time, don’t believe everything you read. MacKeeper is a great example of an antivirus program that has got a bad rap, but it’s worked hard to repair its reputation. It has gained Apple Notarization, which means the software has been checked by Apple for malicious components, and the company has garnering certification from various bodies to prove it isn’t a PUP (potentially unwanted program), including an AV-Test certificate. That said, we haven’t recommended it here, and that’s simply because we feel that there are better options available. If you have already installed MacKeeper and wish to try one of our alternative recommendations, we explain How to uninstall MacKeeper.





6.
What can’t Mac antivirus protect you from?
Using a Mac antivirus product, especially one that includes tools to improve your online privacy, may lull you into believing you’re completely safe from personal and private information leaking out and that you no longer need to keep your wits about you. That’s not quite the case. While there’s no reason to panic, you should still practice caution – and there are a few more issues you should consider when using Mac antivirus, too.
First, an antivirus for Mac product may upload the complete text of files flagged to the cloud, where it can be analyzed by separate tools hosted there. This practice is normal and sensible: some malware can detect when a running process may examine it, and will then engage in subterfuge. Antivirus software makers also can access their massive databases to examine files with characteristics that trigger their algorithms – certain elements that match known malware. As a result, security researchers discover new viruses, worms, Trojans horses, and the like. However, helping the greater good means you’ll have to be comfortable with trusting a third-party with your file contents. Where appropriate, we noted privacy policy issues in individual reviews.
Second, this software may also rely partly or entirely on cloud-based checks of URLs, malware, and the like. Accordingly, an antivirus package might upload every URL you visit, metadata about files, signatures of files, information about your computer’s hardware, a list of running or installed applications, and more. Companies vary on their disclosure of such policies, and may not let you opt out of this kind of sharing. We note issues in each review as appropriate.
Third, antivirus software makers also get a sense of what behavior is happening on your computer that’s being monitored or blocked, and may use that information for their own purposes. In some cases, you can opt out of this information gathering.





7.
What virus cleaner does Apple recommend?
Apple has never recommended a third-party virus cleaner, and has instead focused on the Xprotect and Gatekeeper functions found within macOS, which are regularly updated with operating system updates.





8.
How good is Apple’s virus protection?
It’s actually very good, and there isn’t much that gets past it in the way of viruses and malware, given its Xprotect and Gatekeeper features – but these can be overridden, and questionable software can be installed and activated if the user knows what they’re doing.
Still, the protection is present, it’s updated well, and Apple keeps a good eye on things, but new viruses and malware are sent out from bad actors all the time, and this is where a good third-party application can come in handy.
We have tested Apple’s own solution against a range of malware samples. While it did a reasonable job overall, we found instances where questionable applications could be installed without any warning. A helpful analogy is to think of Apple’s built-in antivirus system, XProtect, as the lock on your Mac’s front door, while a paid antivirus solution acts more like an alarm system with security cameras. Third-party tools update their virus definitions – including not just viruses, but also adware, spyware, trojans, and ransomware – several times a day, often more frequently than Apple’s protections, providing real-time defense against new and emerging threats.
During our testing of Apple’s malware protections, recovery options were limited. In some cases, the only solution was to wipe the Mac and restore from a backup made before the risky behavior – hoping nothing had already spread. Apple does not offer dedicated malware removal support or guarantees if an infection occurs, nor does it protect against cross-platform threats across multiple devices. Paid antivirus software typically includes these services, along with additional features such as web and phishing protection, vulnerability patching tools, VPNs, password managers, parental controls, secure cloud backup, and dark web monitoring.
That said, macOS’s built-in security may be sufficient for low-risk users who install apps only from the App Store or trusted developers, keep automatic updates enabled, avoid pirated software, do not disable Gatekeeper, have limited exposure to risky email attachments, and do not handle sensitive client data.
Ultimately, investing in a reputable security suite for Mac adds an extra layer of protection – and for many users, it’s a case of being safe rather than sorry.





9.
Is there free virus protection for Mac?
The Xprotect and Gatekeeper functions serve as free virus protection for macOS, but you can also get basic virus protection from many of the well-known antivirus providers, we have some recommendations above. 





10.
How to choose the best Mac antivirus for your needs
There are a lot of Mac antivirus programs to choose from. What you want is one that offers a familiar and easy-to-use interface that works well on a Mac – a key reason why we recommend Intego’s antivirus. You should also look for antivirus with a good detection rate – not just for Mac viruses, but also for PC viruses, unless you want to be passing viruses on to friends and clients running Windows. Low impact on system resources is also critical, especially if your Mac isn’t the most powerful model.
Consider the type and number of devices you want to protect – are you looking for an app to cover one Mac, or Mac, iPhone, iPad and even a PC? Your budget matters here, too: do you prefer a subscription model or a one-time payment?
Mac antivirus vendors typically offer different add-ons, and it is certainly a case of you get what you pay for: free products will have fewer bells and whistles, but the most comprehensive Mac security suites will include password managers, parental controls, cloud storage and more. The underlying antimalware engine will usually be the same for all security products from a particular company, so you can save money if you don’t need all those extra features.





11.
When are Apple’s built-in protections sufficient
For many users, Apple’s layered security – XProtect, Gatekeeper and Rapid Security Responses – is more than adequate. If you fit into the “low-risk” category described below, you can probably rely on macOS alone.
You only download apps from the Mac App Store or trusted developers. Gatekeeper ensures that only notarized software from identified developers can run, and XProtect scans these apps for known malware on launch.
You keep automatic updates enabled. Apple regularly updates XProtect’s malware definitions in the background, and with macOS Tahoe, Background Security Improvements can now install critical patches silently without requiring a restart.
You avoid pirated software, torrents, and “cracks.” These are common vectors for malware that can bypass Apple’s checks if a user overrides warnings. 
You do not handle sensitive client data or work in a high-risk environment. For casual home use, the built-in tools are generally enough to block the most obvious threats





12.
When paid Antivirus is worthwhile
Despite Apple’s strong foundation, there are clear gaps that third-party software fills.
You frequently install software from various internet sources. In our hands-on testing, we have found that it is still possible to install malware by ignoring or bypassing Gatekeeper warnings. Our testers were able to install trojans, fake apps, and software that requested access to the microphone, webcam, and keystrokes.
You want protection against phishing and malicious websites. Apple’s XProtect primarily focuses on known malware files. It does not offer the same level of real-time web and phishing protection that suites like Avast One or Bitdefender provide.
You need more frequent updates and broader threat coverage. Third-party tools update their virus definitions several times a day, often more frequently than Apple’s updates. They also cover a wider range of threats, including adware, spyware, trojans, and ransomware.
You want features like a firewall, VPN, password manager, or identity monitoring. Apple does not offer a dedicated, configurable firewall for macOS (it relies on the built-in one) and does not include a VPN, password manager, or dark web monitoring in its security suite. Paid suites bundle these features.
You share files with Windows users. An unprotected Mac can unknowingly harbor Windows viruses that won’t affect macOS but can be passed on to friends and colleagues. A good antivirus will detect and clean cross-platform threats.

title: Things 3.25 for Mac Gains Touch Gestures
content:
Cultured Code today released Things 3.25 for Mac, bringing full optimization for the PROLED MacBook Pro to its task management app.


Since the touchscreen MacBook Pro launched, all Mac apps feature basic touch input, with taps performing the equivalent of mouse clicks. Things already worked with that default behavior, but Cultured Code says version 3.25 fully optimizes the app for touch with additional gestures, improved dragging, and larger controls.

A rightward swipe on a to-do opens the scheduling dialog, while a leftward swipe selects or deselects it. Users can also select several items by moving two fingers up or down through a list. To open a to-do, users can tap it to select it and tap again to expand it, or double-tap.

Cultured Code says dragging to-dos and headings is smoother and more responsive, whether moving one item or a group. Holding a finger on an item in a selection picks up the whole group, rather than only that item. The update also improves how dragging works when some selected items are outside the visible area of the list.



Custom menus and date pickers adapt to the input method, showing more spacious rows and larger touch targets when opened with a finger. Buttons elsewhere in the app also have larger tap targets.

Other changes make it easier to resize the sidebar by touch and rearrange checklist entries within a to-do. Users can cancel either a to-do or an individual checklist entry by pressing and holding its checkbox. The release also includes smaller adjustments to touch interactions and interface polish throughout the app.

title: Apple might make the iPhone 18e’s camera bump much bigger
content:
Macworld





For as long as Apple has been making budget iPhones, they’ve had single cameras. And for as long as iPhones have had single cameras, they’ve been positioned all alone in the top left corner.
According to a new report by Filipe Esposito at Engadget, however, that’s going to change with the upcoming iPhone 18e. Apple is reportedly going to add a small squarish camera array to house the iPhone 18e’s camera components.
Apple uses square arrays on products that have more than one visible sensor. For example, the iPad Pro, while having just a single 12MP wide-angle camera, has a square array to house the camera, flash, ambient light sensor, microphone, and LiDAR scanner. By contrast, the iPad Air has the same 12MP camera as the iPad Pro, but without an array. Instead, it has a single camera and microphone in the top right corner.
The iPhone 17e has a similar setup to the Air and the previous “e” and “SE” phones that came before it. The rear design is stark, with a single camera lens, microphone, and flash at the top right.
Assuming this is the direction Apple has chosen, it’s not clear what this change will add to the phone. For one, the array will appear rather empty with just a single camera. For another, the look won’t match any of the current iPhones, and it will upset the otherwise clean look of the iPhone 18e. In fact, it could make the 18e appear somewhat outdated, since Apple hasn’t used a square array on an iPhone since the iPhone 15. 
The iPhone 18e is expected to arrive in March alongside the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

title: EU in Talks With Apple Over Barriers to Rival iPhone Browsers
content:
The European Commission is in talks with Apple over rules that developers say stop them from offering browsers powered by their own technology on the iPhone.


The discussions follow an open letter published yesterday by Mozilla, Shopify, and a coalition representing up to 55,000 EU businesses and organizations. They argue that Apple has technically opened the door to competing browser technology, but made it too difficult to use in practice.

The dispute concerns what happens beneath a browser's interface. Firefox on the iPhone looks different from Safari, but both use Apple's WebKit engine to display websites. Mozilla wants to use its own engine, Gecko, which powers Firefox on the Mac and would let it bring additional Firefox features to the iPhone.

began allowing alternative engines in the EU with iOS 17.4. Mozilla argues Apple's conditions mean it cannot simply switch existing Firefox users to Gecko via an app update. It would need to release a second Firefox app, then persuade users to download it and manually move their bookmarks, passwords, and browsing history.

The coalition says no browser maker has managed to move its existing EU users from WebKit to its own engine more than two and a half years after Apple's deadline to comply with the Digital Markets Act (DMA). It wants the European Commission to open formal proceedings and force Apple to remove the alleged barriers.

POLITICO's Fair Play newsletter that it is "currently in dialogue with Apple." The Commission is also consulting the signatories about how rival browsers can compete with Safari on Apple devices. It described browser competition as a DMA priority because browsers determine how people access the web and how publishers reach their readers.

requirements for competing engines protect users from malicious websites and other security threats. Developers seeking approval must meet privacy and security standards and commit to fixing vulnerabilities promptly.

What you need to know…
Apple released the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro in October, while the M5 Pro and M5 Max models got a higher-end option with a touchscreen PROLED XDR display and a lighter design at a $400 premium over the existing models. If you don’t want the better display, we expect the older M5 Pro and M5 Max models to see significant savings over the Black Friday weekend. 
Meanwhile, the M6 model is just a chip upgrade. An older M5 MacBook can still be good value, but a small discount alone doesn’t make it the better buy. Compare its price with the newer model with the same screen size, memory, and storage. If the difference is small, consider whether the newer model’s improvements justify the extra cost. An older model with more memory or storage may be more useful to you than a newer model at a similar price.
Even with an M5 chip, the MacBook Air is still an excellent laptop for just about everyone. Amazon already dropped prices by $200-$250 in early November, which is the lowest we’ve seen since prices went up in June. We’ve seen prices for the 13-inch model with 512GB of storage drop as low as $1,099, so we’ll be on the lookout for it to drop under $1,000. Fingers crossed.
Speaking of under $1,000, this is also the first Black Friday that Apple’s budget MacBook Neo is available. Released in March, it has an A18 Pro processor, 8GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage for $699, although back in March that was just $599 until Apple increased the price in June. There hasn’t been much in the way of sales since then (the best we’ve seen has been about $30 off), but we’re hoping to see $50 or even $100 off over Black Friday, especially with rumors of a new model arriving early next year.

Finally, the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio also arrived this fall at significantly higher prices than the previous model. The M5 Max now starts at $2,499, $500 higher than before, while the M5 Ultra costs at least $5,499, a whopping $1,500 higher than the M3 Ultra’s $3,999 starting price. There may be deals – we’ve seen discounts as much as $200 – but if you don’t need that kind of power, you’re better off sticking with the iMac or Mac mini.

On top of that, all iPads got price hikes of $100-$200 in June, so you can expect to pay more than you would have last year for the same tablet, even on sale.
The lone exception is the iPad mini. In October, it got a massive overhaul with an 8.5-inch OLED display, thinner design, landscape FaceTime camera, IP67 water resistance, and an A20 Pro processor. It starts at $699 now, compared to the previous generation’s original price of $499. Just note that in 2026 Apple updated the AirTags, so make sure the deal you are looking at is for the 2nd generation, or that it compares favorably with the new models.

At Macworld we’ve been covering and reviewing Apple and Apple devices for more than 40 years, from the original Macintosh to the most recent M6 MacBook Pro and iPhone 18 Pro. PRICES CHECKED 24 NOVEMBER 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy an iPad, with discounts spanning affordable everyday tablets, powerful Pro models, and clearance stock from previous generations. This year’s standout Black Friday iPad deal so far is on Apple’s newest tablet. Amazon has listed the 128GB iPad mini (A20 Pro) for $599 in the U.S., $100 off. 
For most people, we’d recommend the 11-inch M4 iPad Air. Amazon has listed the 128GB Wi-Fi model for $649 in the U.S. and £669 in the U.K., saving $100 and £80, respectively. If you mainly want an iPad for browsing, streaming, or schoolwork, the 128GB A16 iPad at $379 is the cheaper U.S. option. It’s $20 below its October Prime Day price, although it still costs $30 more than it did before Apple raised prices in June. 
The biggest savings are on configurations with more storage. Amazon has listed the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 1TB for $1,499 in the U.S., and the 512GB version for £1,199 in the U.K., saving about $300 and £200, respectively. Those are worth a look if you need the extra space. If you don’t, a lower-capacity model may still cost less. See our best Apple Black Friday deals for more.
From November 27 to 30, Apple will include a $100/£80 Apple Gift Card when you buy an 11-inch or 13-inch M4 iPad Air directly from Apple, or a $125/£100 Apple Gift Card with an 11-inch or 13-inch M5 iPad Pro. The standard A16 iPad and iPad mini are excluded. Apple is also offering a $25/£20 gift card with eligible purchases of the Apple Pencil Pro or a Magic Keyboard for the iPad Air or iPad Pro. The gift card is for a future purchase. See our full guide to Apple’s Black Friday.
Which iPad should you buy this Black Friday?


M4 iPad Air – Our best all-round choice

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Air offers a strong balance of performance, screen size, and price without the premium cost of the Pro. The 11-inch model suits buyers who prioritize portability, while the 13-inch version gives you more room for multitasking and creative work.
A good Black Friday discount could make either size an attractive purchase. Compare storage capacities carefully, though: a larger advertised saving on a high-capacity model isn’t necessarily better value if you don’t need the extra space. 
U.S. Black Friday price: At Amazon, you can already get a saving of $100 off some iPad Air models, although in some cases these are selling out, in which case we are seeing Best Buy match the $100 off.  
U.K. Black Friday price: Amazon has either £80 or £90 off most configurations of iPad Air. For example, you can get the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB for £669, down from the usual £749. These are reasonable savings, although we saw better discounts during October Prime Day, with up to £144 off. Last Black Friday, selected M3 Air configurations received £100 discounts.
Apple’s deal: You can get a $100/£80 Apple Gift Card when you buy an 11-inch or 13-inch M4 iPad Air from Apple, which is similar to the Amazon U.K. deal. 






iPad Pro – Best for demanding creative work

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Pro is the option for buyers who need Apple’s highest-end tablet performance and premium display. It comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, but its capabilities – and price – will exceed what many people need for browsing, streaming, and everyday apps.
We’d look for a substantial saving rather than buy simply because it’s the most powerful iPad. Compare discounted M4 iPad Pro models, too: an older Pro could offer better value if its price is sufficiently below the equivalent M5 configuration. 
U.S. Black Friday price:  During October Prime Day, the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 256GB was $1,099, saving $100. So far we’re seeing nearly $300 off a 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro.
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought little to recommend on the M5 iPad Pro, with reductions of around £12. Last Black Friday, older M4 iPad Pro offers included a saving of approximately £206 at Amazon. Amazon has the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 512GB for £1,199 (£200 off). That matches its pre-June RRP and is £100 above its previous low of £1,099.
Apple’s deal: You can get a $125/£100 Apple Gift Card with an 11-inch or 13-inch M5 iPad Pro.






iPad (A16) – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Apple




The A16 iPad remains a capable option for browsing, streaming, schoolwork, and everyday use. However, Apple raised its starting price by $100/£100 in June, and it doesn’t support Apple Intelligence.
That makes the final purchase price particularly important. A modest discount from today’s higher asking price may still leave you paying more than this iPad previously cost. With a replacement expected early in 2027, we’d look for a substantial Black Friday saving and compare the price with discounted iPad Air models before buying.
U.S. Black Friday price: This Black Friday we are seeing $70 off the 128GB iPad. The current $379 price is lower than October’s $399 price. We don’t expect it to go any lower.
U.K. Black Friday price: October coverage listed the 256GB model at £499.97, around £29 off. Last Black Friday, the 128GB version was £299 and the 256GB version was £399. We hope to see even lower prices this year, but so far Amazon has the 128GB model for £399 and the 256GB model for £499, both £30 off. 






iPad mini with A20 Pro – Best for portability

				
					

				
			
Apple




The new iPad mini went on sale on November 6, replacing the A17 Pro model. It brings an 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, and a thinner, lighter design, making it the option to consider if you want a compact iPad with the latest hardware.
Because it has only just arrived, we’d expect initial discounts to be smaller than clearance savings on its predecessor. The older A17 Pro mini could still be worthwhile at a sufficiently low price, but compare the saving with what you give up – particularly the new display.
U.S. Black Friday price: The A20 Pro mini wasn’t available during October Prime Day or last Black Friday. Amazon has it for $599, $100 off and the best price we’ve seen so far. Its 128GB A17 Pro predecessor was $499 during October Prime Day and $399 last Black Friday. You might be able to get a good deal on that 128GB A17 Pro iPad mini, which was $449 earlier in November, but it is now back at $499 at Amazon. 
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought only a small saving on the A17 Pro mini. The 128GB version reached £399 earlier this year, though – before Apple pushed up prices. You can still get the A17 Pro iPad mini for £100 less than the new model, but we hope to see bigger savings as Black Friday approaches.
